#9961. 30 years of Internet transfers with curl

Thirty years ago, on November 11, 1996 the young Brazilian student Rafael Sagula posted the source code for his tiny HTTP download tool online. That was httpget 0.1: a little over 100 lines of C code. Bare bones source code with almost no error checks and limited functionality.

When I found the source code of that initial httpget release just days after Rafael put it online, I had no idea how HTTP worked. The language to speak over the network to ask for resources. Okay, I already knew we call it protocol but not a lot more. I also had never heard of neither httpget nor Rafael before. I imagine that I found httpget by searching on Altavista since this was before Google, but I can’t recall the details.

Seeing the simplicity of this code it was not difficult to immediately spot the fundamental basics of the protocol. I presume maybe in the same vain how countless others in decades to follow also have thought of it when seeing the details for the first time. Much later I would come to understand that to be an illusion of simplicity, but in those early days I was more amazed and fascinated. I already enjoyed doing network programming and HTTP reasoned with me at once.

httpget 0.1 was almost completely without error checks and it used plain IPv4 addresses; no hostnames or URLs.

I, still a naive and enthusiastic developer with an Open Source mindset (even though that term would not be established until 15-16 months later), addressed some immediate bugs I ran into and added name resolving to the tool. I made diffs and emailed patches over to Rafael; the standard way we exchanged code changes back then. I knew about RCS and CVS for version control, but the use of these tools was spotty. It would actually take until September 1999 until I adopted CVS fully for the curl project. We later switched to using git in 2010.

The average internet connection speed of a normal household in Sweden, where I lived and I still live, in 1996 was 30 kbps. 30 kilobit per second. This was before v90 came and bumped the modems up to 56 kilobits. Ordinary mortals connected to the internet using modems over their single phone lines. Today, the average Swedish connection speed is 200 megabits/second.

Thirty years ago there were just 36 million global Internet users and 250,000 websites. Compared to the 6 or 7 billion users and 1 billion websites of today.

We used simpler protocols and while encrypted protocols like SSL existed, they were not used a lot and only for a few rare sites.

In November 1996, my main home computer was still an Amiga 3000 powered by a 25Mhz 68030 CPU but in early 1997 I upgraded to a faster and more modern machine: an Intel Pentium 120Mhz. I ran Windows 95 on this thing, and its prime use was to run an X server so that I could connect to my work computers and pop up X11 terminals at home. I built the first versions of httpget remotely on SunOS, Solaris and Dell Unix – because they happened to be what we had running at work.

I installed and tested Linux for the first time at work in 1997. I got our first public web servers up and of course I made sure curl worked fine on it. I did not switch to Linux on my home machine until 2000 when I also updated to an Intel Pentium III 733 Mhz box.

In 1996 I was working as a software developer doing embedded systems and Unix development in C, for a small Swedish company called Frontec Railway Systems. While working there, I came to learn about and enjoy IRC, and in my spare time a few friends and I developed an IRC bot we called Dancer. Spare time developing a TCP client written in C.

As the IRC bot slowly grew more capable, I wanted to use its extension capability and provide a currency translation service for the participants in the channel (the IRC term for a chat room). In an international channel like ours, we frequently discussed the price of things and having the bot able to quickly explain how much a hundred German Marks equaled in US Dollars could be a useful service.

My currency service needed to update currency rates maybe once per day so that it could use decently accurate rates. I found an HTTP page listing a bunch of currency rates and the httpget tool for doing the downloads, and then the bot could offer up-to-date currency rate translations. All was good.

I discovered computers and programming as a teenager on a Commodore 64. I got hooked immediately. I first learned Basic and moved on to 6510 assembler pretty quickly. In the late 1980s me and my friends had demo groups where we would write cool demos (and some game attempts) in assembler (under the group name Horizon). I established my habit of spending spare time on programming back then.

In the early 1990s I moved over to Amiga, started writing a text editor, got my first job at IBM where I truly got into a lot of C and Unix for the first time. Together with some friends we ran a BBS (The Holy Grail), for which we eventually would write our own BBS software; me and my brother Björn. I learned Motorola 68000 assembler on the Amiga. I wrote 8086 assembler on PC.

I never attended university. I got my first computer job at IBM when I was twenty. I then thought I would take the uni route later, but I never did. I remain uneducated.

In the early 1990s I discovered both the Internet and the world of freely available source code and I was hooked.

Rafael was not terribly keen on dealing with my patches for httpget. I believe he mostly just put his code out without any particular desire to do anything more with it. Instead I became the httpget maintainer and kept polishing it. My main project was Dancer, the IRC bot. httpget was just a side-project to make sure the currency service kept working fine.

At some point I fell over a gopher site that provided many more currency rates than the HTTP page I was scraping at the time so of course I had to add support for that as well to the download tool. With gopher support added, it was not just http anymore and the name of the tool was no longer accurate. It became urlget. A third listing was found that provided rates over FTP and, yes, I added support for that protocol as well.

Already from the start I made the source code available under a free license, continuing what Rafel kicked off. He hosted the first releases, but during 1997 I took over and hosted the tarballs on the website I set up and administrated for work. I told my friends and the news about the tool slowly spread. I started getting bug reports from users and occasionally someone sent me patches to fix problems or add features.

This was a time of many Unix flavors and as I wanted widest possible use and adoption, I knew that I needed help and assistance from friends to make sure it built and ran fine on all those different systems.

In the beginning of 1998 I added upload support to the urlget tool (both FTP upload and HTTP POST) and again I realized the name of the tool was wrong. I decided I should try a name that contains the word URL, that can be pronounced in English and that is easy (and short) to type on a keyboard. cURL it was.

The leading ‘c’ could be short for client but I also liked that the name could be pronounced as see URL, as the tool would display the resource at the URL. You would see it (in a terminal). Naming things is hard.

curl 4.0 was released on March 20, 1998. By then it had grown to 3,300 lines of code and it featured 24 command line options and it spoke three protocols.

Gradually I lost interest in the IRC bot and the currency service but I stuck with curl. People used it, I got feedback, it improved.

I started and participated in several other Open Source projects, but curl remained my main baby and focus.

The concept of a function library that offers useful functionality to other programs is a concept I learned already on my Amiga days. As an example, I wrote the scripting language (FPL) for our Amiga text editor (FrexxEd) as a library, and we could later use that language for our BBS software, FrexxLink (which ran on OS/2) as well as in Dancer, the IRC bot.

A library is sort of next-level cool: not only is the source code available for everyone, but the functionality is as well; in an easy-to-use way.

The idea of converting curl into a library was already in the back of head from the start and in the summer of 2000 I refactored the internals and in August that year we introduced the first ever libcurl. Maybe someone else wants to do Internet transfers in their services or tools? Turns out some did!

One of the first adopters of libcurl was the PHP language which almost immediately decided that libcurl would become their default internet transfer engine. Being a key component and therefore part of their success journey helped getting users, getting testing, bug reports, feature requests and making the library solid.

curl is a child of the 1990s. Back then there were not a lot of options and language alternatives if you wanted to write a program that would easily build and run on most available operating systems and CPU architectures. Sure, C++ maybe could have been an option but I never liked it – and I still don’t. I’m also a strong believer in continuous and non-stop improvements and iterations; not rewrites. curl was never rewritten and if I get my way, it never will be. We do however repeatedly refactor and rearchitect internals to adapt to a changing world.

I wanted curl to be usable by everyone on every machine so it was designed and written for that purpose from the start. The source code in a portable way and the license in a liberal way.

We did most things wrong at the beginning but we learned, adapted, tried again, iterated and we kept doing release after release. Gradually we learned and did better. Every release with lots of bugs fixed and often a few new features. I kept spending my spare time on curl. Every day, every week, every year. Given enough time, something great can grow.

I did my first twenty-three years of this journey with curl only as my hobby. While curl happened, life also happened in parallel. I have switched jobs many times. I got married, bought a house, got two kids, and saw the kids grow up to be amazing adults. Somewhere in there I also managed to convert my hobby into my full time job. Living the dream.

curl is my life. My life is curl. I have been invited and able to speak to audiences hundreds of times in a dozen countries. I have received multiple awards and even gold medals straight from the hands of royalties for my open source work.

I don’t have an end goal with curl and I never did. I just want it to do internet transfers the best way possible: fast, securely, using the proper protocols in optimal ways. There is no rush towards anything. It is just a non-stop walk forward with never-ending polish and tightening every bolt there is.

Thirty years have flown by and yet the development pace is still intense. We regularly implement new transfer protocol features before anyone else. We have leading implementations for lots of network solutions. We ship code that carries a huge portion of the world’s internet infrastructure on its shoulders without fuss.

I still enjoy building things. Writing code to create something that did not exist before; and maybe even more so to make the program actually do things users want and like. I enjoy fixing bugs partly for that reason, but I also like the puzzle and the challenge of debugging and solving tricky problems. Designing a software architecture, coming up with APIs and figuring out how to provide powerful network transfer functionality to power billions of devices are things that make me eager to get started again every morning – still after thirty years.

It never really gets done. The world of the Internet and its transfers keeps changing. New protocols, new versions, new flavors, new third party libraries, new build tools and environments force us to constantly change and adapt.

I want curl to be a leader in internet transfers, its protocol implementations and every aspect of the project. I want us to be an exemplary Open Source project and run every tiny piece of it in an almost excessively transparent and progressive way. curl should be a top contender for the most-secure software component you can find. Our project should be friendly and welcoming to newcomers, both users and developers and not the least, there can be no other software project to compete with the amount, the accuracy and the plethora of documentation. Not to mention that we never break APIs or ABIs. Applications and scripts should be able to keep running, unmodified, even when they upgrade curl. Until the end of times.

I’m a firm believer in iterating and never rewriting. We fix, we refactor and we clean up but rewriting into another language or even using the same language is out of the question.

Simply put: software engineering done right.

While curl speaks more than two dozen protocols (at least counting URL schemes), it has always been most known for HTTP(S) and I think we put the most work and efforts into its HTTP engine. We know lots of people use curl for debugging HTTP in general and their server implementations in particular. We were early adopters of both HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. We are often told people use our way of speaking HTTP and our source code as guidance for how things should be done. This is an honor and a huge responsibility that we take seriously.

After I first had learned about HTTP from reading httpget source code and then of course studied the RFC documentation explaining the specifics. In the late 2000s I learned about the HTTPbis effort and joined the mailing list for the HTTP specification update in the works. In 2009 I participated in my first ever IETF meeting that took place in Stockholm, Sweden. There, I got to meet some of the HTTP RFC authors and main people for the first time: Roy, Larry, Mark, Julian etc. They are all lovely people and I really felt that I would be able to make curl better by hanging out in the HTTP IETF circles more. I also wanted to contribute back my own experiences and viewpoints to maybe help improve the world ever so slightly.

That community later started the HTTP Workshop series out of which I have been to every single instance. Hanging out with the primary HTTP implementers in the world is fun, super educational and humbling. I believe this networking makes HTTP and all the involved  implementations even better.

curl is not a legal entity or a formal organization of any kind. It is a bunch of loosely connected people on the Internet who have a common goal, a few mailing lists, a website and some git repositories. curl is not hosted under any umbrella, not part of any larger organization and is not owned or controlled by any company. It is probably as free and independent as a software project can be. I believe this is an excellent position for curl and gives us maximum flexibility and control of our own destiny.

libcurl runs in an estimated thirty billion installations today. It is a rough estimate since the majority of all libcurl users never tell us they use it, but we need to find it mentioned in their credit screens, open source license windows or their manuals. A super popular app might use libcurl today and not tomorrow, or vice versa, which can make the numbers shift by several billions overnight. In reality of course, once the pulse raise has calmed down and your ego is content, these numbers do not matter. In our corner of the world, things don’t change notably when we go from a thousand installs to billions. We still work with similar people, in similar ways, with similar challenges.

For me, and for many others, the coolest place curl has been used is probably on Mars. It was confirmed by NASA that curl was used to aid the Mars landing mission, even if they don’t tell us exactly for what and where.

A ridiculously common question to me is “what is the weirdest place you’ve seen curl run?” I have ceased getting surprised about what devices and what things that are Internet connected and thus where curl runs. Light-bulbs, dish washers, AC units, heat pumps, cars, printers, blenders, ovens, toy robots, drones, guns, motorcycles, medical devices, fridges, soundbars and espresso machines. Of course in addition to all those “traditional” things we already expect to run curl: games, servers, cars, printers, TVs, watches, tablets, game consoles, blue-tooth speakers, routers, mobile phone apps and their operating systems.

Our modern society is keen at eventually making everything network connected, and once they are, they can use curl and libcurl to perform their transfers.

Benevolent Dictator For Life. A term popularly used to describe the steering mechanism of many Open Source projects. Basically a single person being the captain of the ship. The one who can commandeer the direction, who can dictate truths about the project and who says yes and no firmly. For better and for worse, I remain the BDFL for curl. I try to repeat that curl is not a solo-show and it was never a one-man circus. We are literally thousands of people who have contributed code, and every year there are hundreds of new authors helping out. I may remain the captain of the ship, but no ship above a certain size can be managed without a lot of additional man power and curl is no different.

I may very well remain BDFL for a long time to come because I love my role and because I don’t know any other way to live my life or to run the curl project. There are no succession plans and I am against doing such. There is no heir or vice-BDFL prepared to take over. Instead we document everything and every detail so there are no secrets, so that no formal hand-over should be necessary (except for some rare passwords). If I get run over by a truck tomorrow, you guys can figure it out and continue. You don’t need me.

My email address is commonly listed in the regular curl license and this license is usually included in license listings, credit screens or manuals. When random people run into problems or issues with products in this modern society, they often struggle to find someone to help them. There is no one to contact or ask. My email then sometimes serves as a last resort to finally get the answers they’ve been fighting for. I frequently get emails about products I never knew existed, I certainly didn’t know they used curl and I for sure don’t know how to help the users with their problems…

The much darker side of the traces curl usage leaves in products, is when malicious tools, services and attackers use tools that can be associated with me and my email address. I have been accused of various attacks and “hacking” people and companies multiple times. I have received death threats multiple times and I strongly suspect that my US visa problems were triggered by something in these veins.

I stick to the Open Source ethos and spirit. It is a fundamental part of my belief system and I am convinced this is the superior way to produce software to build society on. I do everything I can to stick to the liberal license curl is shipped under because I love the concept. It is however not an easy pitch: give everything away for free and then try to get someone to pay for it. I think it is fair to say that if I wanted to optimize for money, I should have played this one out differently. That would have been another life. Not my life.

Of course I feel immensely proud of what we have accomplished. The little toy thing in 1996 kicked off a journey that led to the creation and continued maintenance of a modern Internet infrastructure cornerstone. We have reached this point, not by talking, not by using marketing nor by tricking someone into using our code. We conquered the world by shipping consistent top quality over several decades. curl runs in all these devices and services done by all those companies because it is the right choice for them, selected because it is Open Source, rock-solid and fast – and also likely to be around in the future. Everyone can depend on us to keep shipping updates in a proven stellar fashion and minimal friction. Forever and ever.

There are many dimensions of the future to consider here. The future of Open Source. The future of curl. The future of internet transfers. The future of the C programming language and the future for me, personally. At least.

I don’t think I can guess the future any better than other humans. I was never good at it and I never really tried to. I always only focus on the next coming months and make quick adjustments when things make turns.

I think Open Source is a solid way to do foundational software, now and in the future. It will continue to have a funding problem and too many projects live and die with a single maintainer. But building common and open building blocks is simply a requirement for speedy development, for building reliable components and for being able to produce products and services at the speed we seem to want. I don’t believe AI will kill Open Source.

I think curl has many more years of service ahead. Primarily because it is the trusted solution and nothing else is even close to this long proven track record, secondarily because it runs on all platforms like no alternatives. I do not rule out that it will be replaced by an alternative at some point, when projects written in C are gradually phased out. (If they ever are.)

Internet transfers in general seem like a fundamental idea that probably is going to be around in a similar style for a long time. The protocols will keep evolving, changing and getting updated but the client/server/protocol concept seems solid and likely to be here for the long term.

I personally will keep working on curl and Internet transfers for as long as I think it is fun and challenging. I turn 56 years old in a few weeks. I hope to be able to spend several more decades on this.

Thank you mom and dad for your understanding and supporting attitude when I as a teenager got completely sucked into a world of computers and programming. Thanks Björn and Kjell for all the awesome times and all the fun when we learned development together and took our first stumbling steps as programmers. Thanks to the Horizon team for the fun and all the demos, copy parties we did and attended. Thanks to Huddinge Vi Unga who owned the machine and sponsored the dual phone connections for our BBS for several years as we discovered fidonet and a world of people and communication. Thanks Jonas for getting me that first job at IBM when I had no work experience at all. Thanks to Bjørn for co-creating the Dancer bot project with me to the people in #amiga IRC chat on Efnet and then IRCnet for your support. Thanks to my bosses at Frontec in the mid 1990s who allowed me to do spare time development on their various Unix machines (even though you probably were not aware of the full extent). Thanks to all the early users and adopters of curl who pushed me forward and who brought it into all the important Linux distros early on and showed me this thing had legs. Thanks Anja, my wife, for keeping up with me spending all this time in front of my machines, and for sometimes boring you to death rambling about some miniscule detail from the curl project that I couldn’t let go from my mind. Thanks to my kids Agnes and Rex for being the lights of my life, for being awesome and for not being particularly impressed by or interested in what I do. You do your life. Thanks to everyone who ever contributed to the curl project, in whatever capacity. In particular, thanks to Stefan, Viktor, James, Viktor, Dan, Jay, Daniel, Max for being part of the core maintainer team for ages. Thanks to Björn, Kjell and Linus of Haxx for being awesome friends and always supporting me and curl whenever it has been needed – and for the Rockbox side-adventure of course. Thanks to Larry at wolfSSL for believing in me and curl enough to allow me to work on curl full-time without even blinking. Thanks to all curl sponsors, donors and to all awesome paying customers of curl support, who combined are what makes it possible for me to do what I do. Thanks to everyone who ever invited me to conferences and events to talk and meet people. Thanks to Patrik who nominated me to the Polhem Prize award that I then received in the form of a gold medal. Thanks Michael for nominating me for the IVA gold medal. Thanks to all others whose names I forgot to include here.

Thanks to everyone who uses curl and continues to participate in curl development.

Yes. We have two separate birthdays: httpget was born in November 1996. curl was born in March 1998.

Rafael Sagula unfortunately left us much too early. He died in 2016. I am grateful for him kick-starting this thing for us.

Irc ! Those were the days. Netscape Navigator and dial-up. What fun. I used Dans mIRC. Oh joy!

#9960. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

#9959. Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft

Says it 'strongly' suspects attack limited to legacy system, and that nothing sensitive is at risk

Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured.

"Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said.

"The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI."

Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations.

Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available.

"Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact.

"As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact.

"Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident."

Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017.

Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy.

Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU).

Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs.

Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days.

In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

#9958. Granite 4.2 LLMs: How They're Built

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

The three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split shows up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:

Granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

The agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

We apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

We then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

Finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

The complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

Before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:

For the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

The 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

Figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

Every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single update behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

Advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

The pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:

What changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:

Parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

The KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:

The 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:

Verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

Each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:

Boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

In the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

Figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

Reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

Figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

Granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

Figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

Figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

Figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

We also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

The FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

The NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

The training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

Granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

OpenCode is an AI coding agent that runs in your terminal.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:

For full documentation, see opencode.ai/docs.

Pi is a minimal agent harness for AI-powered coding that runs in your terminal. It supports custom providers via a models.json configuration file.

Then select the granite-4.2-30b model with /model or Ctrl+L in the interactive session.

OpenHands is an AI software engineer that can plan, write code, and execute commands.

Install and launch OpenHands following the official installation guide.

Configure the LLM in the OpenHands settings with:

Note: The openai/ prefix is required when connecting to OpenAI-compatible endpoints like vLLM. Refer to the OpenHands local LLM documentation for detailed setup instructions, troubleshooting, and alternative installation methods.

Last updated: September 11, 2026 to clarify base models.

#9957. NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

New guidance provides a basic framework for less-technical solo business owners, but it may miss the mark on how to secure technology that requires no human oversight.

Threat actors always target the path of least resistance, and for years that has been small to midsize businesses (SMBs). Now, new guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) aims to help companies with possibly even fewer resources: "solopreneurs."

Cybersecurity White Paper 50 (CSWP) is a series of recommendations on how to curb cyber-risks for a population that makes up 81.9% of all US businesses. NIST is trying to offset challenges with guidance for password hygiene, ransomware threats, and adhering to regulations requirements — areas where solopreneurs typically lack the time, money, or people to build out a security program on their own.

The guide translates its Cybersecurity Framework into lay language for non-employer firms, the agency states. But with 33 pages to work through, is it worth the investment?

Most of the practical core is within reach for solopreneurs, says Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender. People just need to scroll to the short list on page 2, which calls for phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), a password manager, a standard (non-admin) account for daily work, automatic updates, and tested backups with one copy kept offline.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

"None of that needs a security background, and you can do it in an afternoon," Zugec tells Dark Reading.

Compared to other NIST technical publications, Zugec says the CSWP is much easier to digest. Like NIST advertised, the language is plain and every action comes with a reason, a first step, and a note on what changes as businesses grow, he adds.

NIST outlines how businesses can respond to growing contractual agreements and an increasing number of suppliers and third parties as they expand operations and it becomes even more crucial to know third-parties' cyber postures. That means staying current with regulations and establishing a formal process to manage risks that relationships could introduce.

While Bryson Byrd, cybersecurity advisor at Huntress, applauds NIST for the guidance, he says terms like "least privilege," "risk register," and "data sensitivity classification" aren't the language of someone running a bakery or a consulting practice.

"For too long, solopreneurs have been an afterthought in cybersecurity guidance," Byrd tells Dark Reading. "The intent is right, but the closer guidance like this gets to the language of everyday business owners, the more likely it is to actually get implemented."

But it's not just the language, Byrd says. It also assumes the owner knows how to turn on logging, review account sessions, and work though a separate spreadsheet of worksheets. And he points to a recommendation on obtaining legal counsel's input before notifying customers following an incident as an extra cost that often is not in the budget.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

The guidance doesn't appear to take into consideration that "nobody goes into business to build the most secure company that exists," he adds, but to build something over time. Every hour a solopreneur spends on asset inventories, backup testing, tabletop exercises, and compliance tracking is an hour taken away from running the business.

"Asking a single person to do all of this is extraordinarily cumbersome and, quite frankly, unrealistic," Byrd says.

Byrd notes gaps in the guidance in places "we see hurt small businesses in the real world." The first is domain registrar; attackers regularly go after small business domains to launch impersonation attacks and siphon money from customers and partners. Control of the domain means threat actors assume control over email and the business's website.

"Locking down the registrar account with multifactor authentication, enabling registrar lock, and turning on auto-renewal should be part of any baseline for a solopreneur," Byrd recommends.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

The second gap he addresses is email authentication. The three core protocols — Sender Policy Framework, DomainKeys Identified Mail, and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance — are becoming more important to protect a business from being impersonated and to ensure its legitimate email is delivered, Byrd explains.

The third and perhaps most impactful gap for a business of one is what happens when the owner is unavailable for an extended period of time, whether due to an illness, family matter, or simply a well-deserved vacation.

Ransomware groups target businesses during off-hours, weekends, and holidays. If something does happen that demands an immediate response, it's essential for someone to be there. It could mean the difference between an incident and a breach.

"A break-glass plan that gives a trusted person or partner emergency access to critical accounts is still needed, and it belongs in any cybersecurity plan for a solopreneur," he advises.

Previously, SMBs and the self-employed adopted the mindset that they were too small to be considered a target. That has since been disproven and is only worsening.

Advancements in autonomous tools and artificial intelligence (AI) have lowered the barrier to entry and the cost of attacks, letting threat actors target that population at scale. They realized they had a choice: go after large enterprises with strong defenses for one big payout or target thousands of small shops with weak security that are far more likely to pay up.

As the struggles evolved, so must the guidance. Daniel Eliot, lead for small business engagement at NIST, says the new whitepaper comes nearly a decade after its predecessor, NISTIR 7621 rev.1. After the initial call for comments, "that feedback was instrumental in moving the project forward."

AI is forcing a lot of security guidance to be updated and making that guidance easier to write, says Zugec, adding that new CSWP additions include a section on AI and a warning that AI makes phishing more convincing.

NIST urges businesses to take a second or third look at any message that asks people to click a link, download a file, transfer funds, or log into an account.

But contrary to popular belief, AI hasn't brought any new or novel attacks, Zugec says. It is changing who runs businesses and what they rely on to operate.

Solopreneurs are using AI assistants to read their mailboxes, run commands, write code, and use accounts under the owner's identity, he explains. While it enables one person to do the work of a small team, it also expands the attack surface.

"Many solopreneurs will use agentic AI to grow faster than their security does," he says. "The guide gives no advice on what these agents should be allowed to reach or on securing the code they write."

The biggest gap Zugec says he found in the guide is "AI that acts." NIST treats AI as something passive that businesses need to inventory and review outputs for, but agentic AI has increasingly removed humans from the equation.

As agentic AI enables more people to run a business alone, the security of those businesses matters more than ever, Zugec says. That will warrant outside help, as people increasingly turn to vibe coding to build their own applications. He also urges solopreneurs to have their code reviewed by someone with coding and security experience before anything ships.

If anything is public-facing, an attacker can reach it. That warrants protection.

"AI is good at producing software that works but not necessarily software with a small attack surface," he says. "The guide doesn't cover this, yet it's often the first risk solopreneurs run into."

Zugec points out other weaknesses, too. For example, NIST pushed for continuous updates, but a solopreneur can’t realistically track every legal and contractual security requirement, negotiate security terms with a cloud provider, or monitor their systems around the clock.

Second, it never ranks tasks, which makes prioritization difficult for a one-person team. For example, it opens with governance, the least actionable task, while MFA and backup advice only starts on page 14. It also fails to cover two common attack routes: ClickFix, which tricks people into pasting a command themselves, and a malware that steals their logged-in session, which bypasses MFA

"It lists around 25 actions and says outright that it isn't a checklist, so a busy owner has to decide what comes first," Zugec says.

The guide also sets its scope by head count, which is problematic. Technically the head count would be one, but risk follows what information businesses hold and who targets them. But it's not just about size; it's about what's exposed. Risk heavily varies between someone who sells candles on Etsy as a side gig versus someone in the finance industry trading billions in cryptocurrency.

"A solo crypto operator or a consultant with client secrets needs far more than the guide’s baseline," Zugec says.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9956. Apple tells its Support Community to STFU

User-to-user forum goes read-only ahead of November 20 closure, with archive's fate unclear

Apple has abruptly stopped accepting new posts on its Support Community, putting the forum into read-only mode ahead of permanent closure on November 20, 2026.

Users seeking help with their gizmos from other Apple customers were greeted with the message: "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

"We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products."

Need help? Head to the official Apple Support site. Want to see if your fellow Apple users have an answer to what ails your device? This is no longer the forum for you.

Some reports date the site's origins to 1998, when Apple was busy killing off the Newton platform and launching Mac OS 8.5. Technology has come a long way since then, and recent AI developments have made user-to-user forums like Apple's Support Community less popular.

Other places to seek advice remain, and useful answers were never guaranteed. As one user put it on X: "rip to every thread that ended with 'same problem here' and zero solutions."

Still, it's an abrupt end to almost three decades of accumulated advice, troubleshooting, and unanswered questions. Apple hasn't said whether that archive will remain accessible after the closure.

The Register asked Apple for the reasoning behind the termination. The company has yet to respond. ®

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: TornadoVM, A2A Java, Open Liberty, Open J Proxy, Gradle, EclipseStore

Nov 09, 2026 4 min read

This week's Java roundup for November 2nd, 2026, features news highlighting: point releases of TornadoVM, TornadoInsight, A2A for Java, Gradle and EclipseStore; the November 2026 edition of Open Liberty; the third release candidate of Open J Proxy; the second release candidates of Micrometer Metrics and Micrometer Tracing; and the third beta release of Quarkus 4.0.

Build 23 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 22 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

The release of TornadoVM 8.1.0 delivers bug fixes and notable changes such as: the ability for a TornadoVM kernel read and write a device allocation owned by another library owns, in place, without copying it and without writing a TornadoVM array header into it; and a change in the overloaded initializeDeviceAsync() method, defined in the TornadoExecutionPlan class, to initialise a device during application sets up. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Beehive Lab has also released version 2.1.0 of TornadoInsight, their IntelliJ IDEA plugin for TornadoVM. This release includes bug fixes, documentation improvements and new features such as: a new experimental AI-assisted transformation of a Java method into a TornadoVM kernel; and a new TornadoToolchain record that checks the TornadoVM SDK with the project JDK, builds the classpath, compiles with the project JDK, and creates a launcher. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of A2A Java SDK 1.5.0, a Java library that implements the Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) for running agentic applications as A2AServers, ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new OpenTelemetryPushNotificationSenderDecorator class to create a CLIENT enumeration, defined in the OpenTelemetry SpanKind enum class, to reflect the actual delivery outcome of success or failure; and the ability for authorized JPA task listings to offer optional provider capabilities so that supported policies can directly filter both the database count and page queries that for reduced scan and deserialization costs. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The third beta release of Quarkus 4.0.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for Valkey in the Quarkus Redis Client extension; and a new @CheckedTemplateParam annotation to support explicit naming of parameters in methods annotated with @CheckTemplate without the required -parameters compile flag. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The GA release of Open Liberty 26.0.0.11 delivers bug fixes, resolutions to numerous CVEs and new features such as: the ability to configure the timeout of the server quiesce stage, via the quiesceTimeout element, that was once fixed at 30 seconds; and improved validation that blocks form login error page redirects to external hosts unless the target host is listed in the wasReqURLRedirectDomainNames attribute of the element.

The third release candidate of Open J Proxy 1.1.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for PostgreSQL and MariaDB coverage in the C++ ODBC client; and a simplification of building and using the C++ ODBC drivers across all major OS platforms. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of Gradle 9.9.0 provides notable changes such as: the ability for Kotlin DSL scripts to be incrementally compiled using the Kotlin Build Tools API for improved build performance; new test filters that may be applied to JUnit Platform tests that are not declared as methods; and improvements to the Problems API that provides a predefined hierarchy of problem groups from the Problems interface. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of EclipseStore 4.3.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: A refactor of the VectorIndex interface, part of the JVector Index, to handle large indices and concurrent load and crash safety; and a new, lightweight VanillaJS storage viewer for the storage REST Interface that now deprecates the existing standalone Vaadin/Spring-based client GUI. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The second release candidate of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 ships with dependency upgrades and one new feature that adds support for fractional updates in Micrometer Atlas counters that had previously truncated them to a type long. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Similarly, the second release candidate of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: more efficient allocation of OpenTelemetry baggage reads by directly searching retained/current baggage and building the bulk results in one map; and an elimination of allocating wrappers while clearing an already empty context by reusing the NOOP function, defined in the CurrentTraceContext.Scope interface in conjunction with an instance of the Tracer.SpanInScope interface. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Andres Almiray, Java Champion and creator of JReleaser, has introduced his roadmap for JReleaser 2.0. Over the next several weeks, developers can expect changes that include:

A 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT release has been created and there will be numerous breaking changes.
