#9937. Andrew Kensler's permute(), a function for stateless, constant-time pseudorandom-order array iteration

That subtitle is a little bit of a mouthful, but I’ve been wanting to talk about Andrew Kensler’s permute() function for a while and I wanted to make it clear right off the bat why it’s useful. permute() is used some in the graphics community, especially in offline rendering, and the techniques are more widely known in cryptography*, but it’s applicable to so much more than graphics and cryptography.

Let’s first talk about the problem it solves. You want to iterate over \(k\) items of an array of length \(n\), in random order, where \(k \leq n\). Those \(k\) items cannot contain duplicates from the original array (they must each correspond to a unique index). Or, you want to get a random sample of \(k\) items without replacement.

When I say “random”, this is obviously pseudorandom, but there are varying degrees of pseudorandomness. This is unquestionably not cryptographically secure, that’s not its intended use. I can’t say that I know enough about pseudorandomness to say how statistically indistiguishable from random this is or for what applications it will be random enough. It’s good enough to use for computing rendering integrals, and I’d be comfortable using it for a lot of casual statistical analysis.

Update May 27, 2021: I saw what looks to be a nice improvement to the randomness of this, and extends it to work for 64-bit integers. I recommend taking a look after reading this post!

Anyway, the canonical way to randomly iterate over an array is to first shuffle it with the Fisher-Yates shuffle, and then iterate over the shuffled array.

*I found this Stack Overflow answer from 2009 that gives the exact same idea, so I should be clear that Andrew Kensler didn't really invent the method I'll talk about here, but I think he popularized the use of it in graphics and certainly created the particular hash function I'll show at the end.

uniform_rand_int(min, max) is inclusive of both min and max, i.e. \(\textnormal{swap\_idx} \in \{i, i+1, \dots, n-1\}\)

Obviously this manipulates the array in place, which may not be desirable for a bunch of reasons. In practice you might call this with an array of indices or an array of pointers.

There are a bunch of situations where the Fisher-Yates shuffle doesn’t work very well, because you need to store the shuffled array.

In the latter two cases there’s obviously a lot more to think about, like the cost of just reading incoherent values from the large array. There are other good ways to solve #2 and #3 too, especially if you’re doing distributed computing. But a lot of the techniques I know share the problem that you need to scan over the entire array at least once. If you have constant-time access into the array, Kensler’s method is always linear only in the size of your random sample, not in the original array.

In other words, if you want to iterate over \(k\) random, unique items from an array of length \(n\), then the Fisher-Yates shuffle is \(O(n)\) time and \(O(n)\) memory. As I’ll show in a second, this can be reduced to \(O(k)\) time and \(O(k)\) memory. But permute() is \(O(k)\) time and \(O(1)\) memory, the best you could possibly do. Not only that, but with permute() you can arbitrarily query random indices in constant time, which means you can use it in parallel across multiple threads or computers.

I think it’s worth mentioning you can extend the Fisher-Yates shuffle to handle #2. You use a sparse map to keep track of swapped indices rather than putting them into the array. When you swap the next index, you check your map to see if the original or swapped locations in the array have already been swapped. If so, you use the values from the map, otherwise you just use the original indices, and then you update the map. Here’s a code snippet to show what that looks like. This will select \(k\) random unique integers from the values \(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}\).

But still, even this “incremental” Fisher-Yates shuffle requires \(O(k)\) memory, which makes it unsuitable for case #1 or case #3.

Update: I believe this is equivalent to, but less elegant than, Floyd's algorithm for random sampling without replacement. So if you want to use that (like if you're in case #2 and really care about good randomness), implement Floyd's algorithm, rather than the way I've framed it here.

Kensler introduced permute() in his paper Correlated Multi-Jittered Sampling. I didn’t quite understand how it worked when I first read it, so I also wanted to write this blog post to break it down and hopefully help others appreciate it. However if you just want the code, skip to the bottom!

The function acts as a “stateless” pseudorandom iterator over an array. It takes in a seed value for a permutation, the length of the array, and the index you’d like to map to a different index. It looks like this:

and if you wanted to use it, say to get 10 random unique values from a vector, you might do:

So how do we construct this magic function?

The first thing we need is a hash function that is invertible for a given power-of-two sized domain. What does that mean? For a given number of bits \(n\), every value from \(0\) to \(2^n-1\) will be hashed to a single unique value in the same range. It’s a one-to-one and onto mapping, i.e. a bijective function. Let’s give a super simple example: adding 1. Let’s say our domain is 2-bit integers. If we add one to a 2-bit number, we’ll get a unique 2-bit number.

Adding is generally, an invertible hashing operation. Another invertible operation in binary is multiplying by an odd number, let’s say 3. \(f(x) = (x * 3) \mod 4\), with:

A non-invertible operation is multiplying by two or any even number:

Kensler outlines more invertible operations in power-of-two domains, especially xor’s and combinations with a seed value, where different seed values give different permutations. Ultimately, we get some invertible hash function:

Already, we can see that this hash will allow us to randomly iterate over an array with length power-of-two. But what about arrays of other lengths? Kensler uses a technique from cryptography called “cycle walking”, which was invented in “Ciphers with Arbitrary Finite Domains” by Black and Rogaway. Cycle-walking is a fancy name, but the idea is simple: we just repeat the hash until the value is less than the length of the array! So we get a permute() function like this:

Obviously this can be really slow since it could take a lot of hashes to get to where we want, but we’ll get to that in a second. First, why does this work at all? This is where the bijective mapping comes in. We start with an index that is less than the length of the array and we hash it until we get another value less than the length of the array. Let’s visualize it like this:

where \(hash^3(x)\) is \(hash(hash(hash(x)))\) or, if you prefer the function composition notation, \(hash \circ hash \circ hash(x)\). In this case, I’ve bolded the first two hashes to indicate that the values are bigger than the length of the array. The last hash is our final permuted value.

Because our hash function is invertible, we can invert the final hashed value (note that we don’t need to actually implement the inverse, this is just theoretical):

By inverting the final value, which was less than the length of the array, we again get a value larger than or equal to the length of the array. So if we did this loop in reverse until we got a value less than the length of the array, we would get back the original index.

In other words, our loop is also an invertible hash function. But rather than mapping within a power-of-two sized domain, it maps within the domain of the array’s length, which is exactly what we’ve been trying to achieve.

We need to make this faster, specifically we don’t want a lot of loop iterations. Let’s say that we have a really good hash function such that there’s roughly a 50% probability that any bit (within our power-of-two domain) will be 1 after hashing. Now, we modify our hash function to specify the power-of-two domain. We do this by taking in a mask that limits the bits which get hashed. Here’s an example (but a bad hash function).

If our hash domain is the two-bit (unsigned) integers, then our mask would be 11 in binary, or 0x3. If our domain is the 32-bit integers, it would be 0xFFFFFFFF.

Now, in our permute() function, we’ll use a mask with all the bits set up to the most significant bit of the highest possible index (that is, len - 1). Here’s a really inefficient (\(O(\log n)\)) implementation for clarity:

However a lot of processors (e.g. x86 processors) have a single instruction that can get the number of leading zeros of an integer. In GCC you can use this with the instrisic __builtin_clz(x), which even on processors that don’t have the instruction will compile to a constant-time operation. So if you use GCC you could write:

This may not be super portable, here is how Kensler does it with bit arithmetic.

With this, our permute() function looks something like:

Because of this mask, we know that our hashing domain is less than two times the size of the array. Since our hash function has a 50/50 chance of flipping the most significant bit, or rather of hashing to a value in the lower half of its domain, we can say that on average, this will take less than two iterations. We’ve got our fast random iterator!

We still need to make a good invertible hash function. As I mentioned, Kensler outlines a bunch of invertible operations, and he uses hill-climbing to find a good hash function. I won’t go into that in more detail, but here is the final code using his hash. I’ve adapted Kensler’s code to the way I’ve structured this blog post:

Okay, there’s one additional thing at the end, the (static_cast(idx) + seed) % len, but that won’t break anything and adds a little extra randomness. The cast to 64-bit is necessary to prevent an overflow bug that could lead to repeats.

I hope that you find this as elegant and useful as I have! One final note: Kensler mentions that this hash only works well up to domains of about \(2^{27}\). For larger domains you could maybe use two calls of the permute function, although if it’s not random enough, that could exacerbate correlations. Overall I really just wanted to present the ideas here.

#9936. PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

As AI accelerates change across the enterprise, PwC's James Shira explains why security teams must rethink their approach to risk and adapt their strategies.

James Shira, global CISO and CIO of PwC, has spent more than two decades navigating the evolution of cybersecurity, from its early days as a largely technical function to its continuously growing role in corporate agendas and spending. Shira's path into the industry was, as he puts it, as "consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow." Originally considering a career in law, Shira decided to pivot, more seriously considering pursuing cybersecurity through independent study, and then formal education. Today, he oversees both technology and security at one of the world's largest professional services firms, giving him a broad perspective on the challenges facing security leaders.

In this episode of Heard It From a CISO with Dark Reading associate editor Kristina Beek, Shira discusses the skills and experience needed to build a career in cybersecurity, including the value of industry certifications, higher education, and on-the-job experience. He also examines the qualities that distinguish effective security teams, the challenges of balancing the CISO and CIO roles, and how security leaders can establish credibility with corporate boards. For Shira, successful leadership comes down to more than technical expertise. It involves building trust, communicating complex issues clearly, and creating an environment where employees can develop.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Shira also shares his thoughts on the topic on everyone's minds: artificial intelligence. He warns that rapid adoption is expanding attack surfaces, adding pressure on security teams, but also notes that AI technology will add opportunities for professionals seeking roles in the field. As for what's ahead, Shira expects significant societal and industry change and shares that this rate of change is likely to be the new standard — it’s best if everyone is prepared to go along for the ride.

This is part of Dark Reading's ongoing Heard It From a CISO video series, which features frank, exclusive conversations with cybersecurity leaders in the trenches. Check out the entire series here.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

James Shira: I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times. But I think that makes for better decisions.

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Dark Reading's Kristina Beek: Hi, everyone. My name is Kristina Beek. I'm an associate editor at Dark Reading, and I'm here for another episode of Heard It From a CISO. Today, I'm joined by James Shira. Thank you so much for joining us. I would love it if you could introduce yourself and talk about your background and your current role as CISO at PwC.

James Shira: Sure. It's great to be with you today. My name is James. I am the global CISO and CIO for PwC. I've been involved in what we used to call IT security since 1999. I became a CISO in the early 2000s, I think 2000 or 2001, really based on an opportunity and happenstance. I've been involved in the community since that time, now 25 or 26 years. For the last eight years, I've also been operating as our global CIO.

DR's Kristina Beek: Love to hear that. How did you first get involved specifically in cybersecurity, technology, or security in general? I know there are a lot of different ways people get involved. Some people study computer science, and some come from very alternative backgrounds. What does your path look like?

James Shira: I think my path is probably as consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow. I was planning on getting a degree to become a lawyer, actually. Then, being a blue-collar kid, I realized I couldn't afford law school. After two years, I needed to make a change, so I redirected toward business and information systems. That was my undergraduate background.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

When I graduated in 1998, there was a bit of a mini-recession, what we often refer to as the dot-com crash. At the time, I used to read the physical Wall Street Journal pretty religiously, and there was a lot of discussion about security. We didn't call it cyber then. I figured this was a space that needed leaders and leadership. I was very interested in working toward and building an executive career path, and I wasn't sure — probably like a lot of college graduates — how to go from having no experience to having an opportunity to be in a role like the ones I'm privileged to have today.

I really started by researching, reading, learning, and studying, a lot of self-directed study, including some computer science-based material. I also did a program at Columbia that's now a master's program, which was very helpful to me. I was one of the first students when we started. The idea was like an MBA for technologists, and I'm proud to say it's now a Master of Science degree. I had the opportunity to be a student mentor there for a long time. It was really on a whim that I thought this space was going to be incredibly interesting, and it's proven to be.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to my next question: What would you recommend to somebody who wants to go into cybersecurity today? In general, what would your advice be? What insights could you provide in terms of what would be best to study? Should they prioritize certifications or a four-year education? There are a lot of different ways to go into cybersecurity today.

James Shira: For sure. I think the four-year education discussion we're all having right now is really relevant. I have younger kids, so I've got some time before they get there. I think it's a really relevant conversation because of the cost. Having worked my way through college and taken out loans at the time, those loan amounts look really small compared with what people are confronted with today. I think it's a very fair question and debate that people should have.

I'm a big proponent of certification on our security team. We really encourage people to do it, and we sponsor some of them. I'm not going to name them because we'd be here for a long time, but I think it's a very smart strategy.

The way I describe it to our folks is that I talk about the concepts of internal equity and external equity. Your internal equity when you come out of college is zero. You're new; you're coming into the industry. You build that up over time with your employer. Obviously, you want to pick the right place to work, as best you can. In the early days, experience in and of itself is the value you're pursuing.

The second piece, external equity, is something you can drive as hard as you want. As a young person without a lot of experience, you can pursue certifications. Some require years of work, but there's a lot out there. The most successful people I've had the privilege to mentor start out with a high degree of emphasis on certifications. Then, after five to seven years of experience, they make a choice about whether they're going to pursue a management track or a higher-end technical director or subject-matter-expert track.

On your question about a four-year education versus certifications, my personal view is that if you want to be in a role similar to mine, or the same as mine, you're going to want that four-year degree. You may even want a master's eventually. If that's your intended path, I would encourage you, notwithstanding the loans, to complete your undergraduate degree. There are a lot of great schools with programs that can be helpful. If you look at that and say to yourself, "That's a significant debt burden, and I don't think it makes sense. I'm not sure I want to pursue being an executive," then I think you should do the certifications and work on getting as much experience as you can.

DR's Kristina Beek: That's a great insight. You talked about building equity and how, when you're fresh out of college, that really depends on your employer and the company you choose to work for. Moving back to PwC, what interested you in the company? Why did you choose to work there, and what has it been like being CISO?

James Shira: When I was coming out of Zurich Financial Services, now Zurich Insurance Group — which was also a great time in my career — I was interested in finding the right CISO challenge at a similar or bigger scale. What interested me about PwC at that time was that it was a 160-plus-year-old institution. I had never worked in professional services; I had only worked in financial services. So a different industry interested me.

I think the organization's values here at PwC were very consistent with mine, and it's been a privilege to be here. It sounds clichéd, but it's really a great place. The quality of people, on average, in my experience, has been really high. People have a desire to do the right thing, and as a CISO, that's incredibly helpful. A lot of our security strategy is culturally centered on employee behavior and training, so those things were very consistent and have been very helpful.

I know some CISOs drive programs through cultures that are less amenable. This culture was incredibly amenable to moving its security program to the next level. Nobody's program is perfect, but that was helpful. Lastly, I had the opportunity to bring a lot of my colleagues with me. I have the privilege of sitting in these roles, but it's not something I did on my own. It's something we've done collectively as a team. Given the scale of the mission here, I had the opportunity to bring some colleagues from my previous employer over, and it's been awesome to see their careers flourish here as well. In short, it's a great place to work.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to a follow-up question. When it comes to a team, whether it's business-oriented or security-focused, what makes a great team? What kinds of people are you looking for, whether in terms of personality or skills?

James Shira: I'm going to answer your question in reverse order. The people I like to work with don't come in a common package. I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times, but I think that makes for better decisions.

The people I'm looking for don't have to have gone to a specific school. They don't necessarily need a traditional profile, but they definitely need to be self-confident and self-directed. I talk to the team a lot about emotional resiliency. I think it's a really important concept in the security industry because, when I got started, security was past the mailroom, past the bathrooms, in the basement somewhere, and rarely in the boardroom. Now, people coming into the field wouldn't even recognize that, because security is such a central, strategically critical issue for companies. I need that confidence in our employees so that, when they become the leaders they can be, they can flourish based on that confidence. It's hard to build a great team without that.

The second piece I think is incredibly important is transparency. It's something I work diligently to practice when I'm speaking in front of the thousands of colleagues I have the privilege of leading: being as brutally transparent as possible about whatever we're trying to do. It's uncomfortable at times, and it can be challenging to answer the questions you get, but I think it provokes the kind of cultural engagement that makes for a great team.

The one thing I'll say lastly is that I don't think mediocrity, as a rule, fits in high-performing teams. You have to embrace your high performers, try to elevate and promote them, and create an environment where they can be as self-directed and successful as they can be.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. When you were answering that, one of the things you talked about was how the CISO role and cybersecurity in general are now in the boardroom. I see a lot of articles about how to communicate with C-suite members as a CISO, how to deal with friction, and how to get your board to believe you. What would you say about communicating your needs as a CISO to the rest of the board? Do you encounter friction in your experience, and how do you deal with that?

James Shira: I think it's a great question. I'm going to offer a point of view. I'll start by saying I've gotten it wrong. I don't have all the answers, but I've learned through mistakes and by having great mentors.

I think credibility with a board starts, frankly, through delivery. The first thing you have to do is build a track record as best you can. That might sound counterintuitive: Don't I need the board's buy-in before I deliver? Somewhat, but I think conversations with our various boards here, and the conversations I've had previously, show that over time, through delivery of the program and driving the change you're advocating for, you can build a lot of credibility.

The second of my three points is that you have to find your own authentic voice. Personally, I'm not a natural. I kind of joke with the team at times that I'm a radio guy, not a TV guy, and I've had to work at being a TV guy. You have to find your own authenticity through your own style. A lot of times, those of us who get the privilege of being in these C-level jobs receive a lot of advice and pressure about how to present and who to be. I would encourage people listening to find their own style and approach that works best for them. Obviously, measure it against how effective it is, but embrace the style that's authentic to you. For me, I just try to be myself with our board.

The last thing I'd say, and I think it's maybe the most important point, is that you have to bring the expertise to the board, not try to drag the board to your expertise. In our domain, don't underestimate how intimidating it can be for the people listening. It's security. They see the headlines. Maybe an issue has occurred in that business. As board members, they feel responsible for providing oversight over management, and they're under tremendous pressure to do so. Don't underestimate that.

If you come at them with a high degree of expertise, terms, acronyms, and things they don't understand, I've found that doesn't work. That would be one of the mistakes I've made in the past. What's worked well for me is not to dumb it down, but to simplify it. If you have enough mastery of a topic, you can describe it in a way that doesn't make the other person feel intimidated and helps them say, "OK, I get that." One suggestion I would offer is to use storytelling. That's what I've done, and it has worked well for me.

DR's Kristina Beek: While you're obviously CISO, you're also CIO, so you have two perspectives. What is it like balancing the responsibilities of both roles?

James Shira: The good news is that, over the last eight years I've had the privilege of being in these roles, there's been a tremendous amount of harmonization between the technology transformation of large enterprises and the need to get the cyber piece right. Therefore, unlike when I started, when security was past the mailroom and in the basement, it's now such a primary issue for organizations that it's really on the CIO's agenda. I think having both of those skill sets is a very critical thing in this day and age.

The one difference I'd acknowledge for the audience, because otherwise anybody watching would think I missed it, is that at times the CIO role can be inherently more political than the CISO role. Let me explain briefly. As a CISO, you objectively know what good looks like: Don't have a breach, don't have an incident, improve your audit posture, drive good risk management, and so on. What good looks like in the CIO world can sometimes be less black and white and more gray. It can change in a way that a traditional CISO might find challenging to navigate.

I, for one, never anticipated the amount of passion and energy that debating different HR or finance platforms might bring. I've learned how to spend a lot of time with CFOs and COOs in our businesses. That's made me not only better professionally, but also more sympathetic to the issues they have, especially in some of the smaller businesses where a decision we might make from a CIO perspective has a significant material impact on their cost basis. There are differences, but in summary, it's a very complementary experience for me. The biggest challenge is time management and moving time between the different things.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. AI is, of course, always part of the conversation. It's changing how attackers work, and it's also changing how organizations operate. What do you see as the biggest cybersecurity opportunity or risk associated with AI right now?

James Shira: I think the most important issue with AI, straight down the middle, is how it changes, evolves, and increases an organization's attack surface. The second issue is the rate of change it brings: how fast it moves and how fast systems have to move. Those are the two dynamics.

What happens to the size of your attack surface? AI can really explode it. At the same time, AI puts pressure on the pace of change across the whole security function. For us specifically, that means dealing with the amount of patching, vulnerability management, inbound requests, and client requests. You have to manage those two dynamics.

On the technology front, in my career — which some people in this audience might think is long, while others might think it's not that long yet — I've never seen anything move as fast. In a short period of time, we've gone from a nascent technology that we're all excited about to actually operationalizing it. At least in my career, I haven't seen anything cross that divide so quickly. Therefore, I think it's ultimately the biggest change-management exercise, maybe ever. That's really where leaders need to center and focus their time.

DR's Kristina Beek: A lot of people are coming out of college or going into college with the expectation of going into cybersecurity or computer science. AI is changing the field very rapidly. A lot of people are scared that they may not even have a job or that there may not be a place for them in this field. What would you say to that, with the rise of AI?

James Shira: I understand where people get that. I understand how people get that. I think it's understandable, but I think it's wrong. The amount of change across society and industries is significant. It's very difficult for me to chart a course in my head for what isn't going to change. Therefore, I think the opportunity for young professionals is to be the change agents — to deliver the change.

I think one thing we don't always do well for our young professionals, but need to, is tell them the truth about the adversity of change management. It's hard. It's hard, and it's going to be hard for them. Do I think AI is a job-elimination technology? I don't. But I understand and respect how people might reach that conclusion.

If you're doing highly repetitive, data-centric activities, that's not, frankly, what you go to college for. Some of us had to do that coming out of college, earning our stripes, but that's not generally what you go to college for. That probably gets changed a lot by AI. Of course. I don't think it's a displacement strategy.

DR's Kristina Beek: Going back to what you said about how AI is changing things so rapidly, what do you think cybersecurity leaders will spend the most time thinking about three to five years from now? I know that's hard because things are changing so quickly, but what do you see for the future?

James Shira: I think the constants I would expect not to go away are the rate of change, the pace, and the pressure. Therefore, I think you have to find consistency in process and strategic principles, meaning how you manage your strategy shouldn't change. You should find the things in executing the strategy and operationalizing it that don't need to change, because so much around you will be changing.

In our history, and in at least my part of the 20-year history of IT security and cybersecurity, when there's been a technical change — think cloud, client-server, mobile, or whatever — we've effectively changed every aspect of how we implemented security controls. I'm hoping and working diligently to avoid repeating that pattern in the AI space because I think it just adds too much volume to an already high-intensity, high-volume situation.

Three to five years from now, I'm hoping AI can be a much more consistent enabler of delivering secure outcomes, but we're still learning how to fully operationalize it. Then there's the issue of token costs, which we're not going to get into today, but that has a high degree of relationship to driving the overall security budget, which we're figuring out as we go.

Secondly, I don't think most companies will have enough money to build a security program the way we've historically done it, at the size and scale that AI could imply would be required. Third, I think organizations are going to have to shrink their digital footprint as they transform. The good news is that — obviously, hope is not a strategy — AI will hopefully allow us to interact with our systems of state much more efficiently than building applications as the recurring front door to all of our systems, as we've done for the last 10 or 20 years. That ought to have a great benefit in reducing the attack surface, too. I think that's what companies need to do, and I think that's what will look so different in three to five years.

Lastly, I'd say I'm expecting significant societal and industry change, especially in a five-year window. I'm not sure I'm going to have a robot at home, but maybe some of us will. I think physical AI is going to place a significant premium on investment capacity, both on the hardware side and on the adoption and implementation side.

There are Orwellian views of that, where you could see the doom and gloom. I think there's also a tremendous opportunity. Some countries are not having the birth rates we need. Frankly, there isn't enough reproduction to maintain the number of people in society. So robots in some places in the world are going to be incredibly helpful in allowing us to deliver the things people need in society.

But I'm excited by it. I'll summarize by saying I think the big fundamental choice you have to make every morning when you wake up is to embrace the change, both in yourself and in how you do the job, because the change is almost — I joked with a colleague the other day, and she's a really capable runner while I am not, that this is kind of like being on the treadmill at the speed Annie would go at, not the speed James would go at. Some days I feel like I'm hanging in there, and other days I feel like I'm about to fall off the back of the treadmill. I think everybody just needs to say that's part of this.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. That's great to hear. Normally, I end these interviews by asking what the future of cybersecurity looks like to you, but we've already touched on that. So I'd rather end with a different question: You've spent a lot of time in tech and security and have seen how it's evolved. What has been the most rewarding part of that work, and what do you think will continue to challenge or motivate you, especially in a field where the risks are sometimes really high?

James Shira: Sure. It's an easy answer for me: It's the people part. It's the team. Every success I've had the privilege of being part of is not a James thing. I had a role, sure, but it's a team thing.

When you see someone — we have a number of people in our organization who started as interns at my previous employer. One colleague started as an intern and is now an executive. Another colleague, Annie, whom I mentioned, is now a partner. Those are the things that lift me back up when I have a bad day, which happens. It's when we see people building and shining in their own way, self-actualizing. That's pretty cool, and I think that's the right way things should work.

Look, it doesn't always work that way. There are probably people on the team who don't feel they got a fair chance, or who feel something didn't go perfectly. That's the challenge of working in teams of people, because people — me, you, all of us — are not perfect.

But the best days for me are when I see colleagues rise, shine, and do great things, and even leave the organization and go do great things somewhere else. That's pretty awesome. I think that's our opportunity with AI and security. We have to embrace it, try to see the positive in it, and grow through it.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. I so enjoyed this conversation. Thank you so much for joining me today.

James Shira: Me too. Thanks for your time.

#9935. Google Summer of Code 2026 results

The Rust Project participated in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for the third time this year. This time we had 13 projects, and our dear contributors have been working very hard on them for several months. As usual, the projects had various durations, so while some of them have ended in August, the last one has only finished in November, so we have been waiting until we have all the results before publishing this blog post.

We are very happy to announce that all 13 projects were successful and passed their final evaluation! We consider it to be a testament to the diligence of our contributors, and the helpfulness of our mentors, that we are able to keep a very high rate[1] of successful GSoC projects several years in a row.

At the start of summer, we had a video call with our contributors, so that we could all get to know each other a bit, and learn about their projects. Over the following few months, we continuously communicated with the contributors, provided guidance and answered their questions and reviewed their pull requests. And most importantly, we learned many new things together! It was an overall great experience. We are grateful for all Rust contributions done by our GSoC participants and for the time we spent working together, and we hope that we will continue seeing at least some of them around in the future.

We would like to thank all our Rust GSoC 2026 contributors. You did a great job!

Even though this year we had fewer projects than in 2025, mostly due to limited mentoring capacity, Google Summer of Code 2026 was again a success for the Rust Project. We think that GSoC is a great way of introducing new contributors to our community, and we are looking forward to participating in GSoC (and other mentorship programs, such as Outreachy) again in the near future. If you are interested in becoming a (GSoC) contributor, check out our GSoC project idea list and our guide for new contributors.

Below you can find a brief summary of our GSoC 2026 projects. You can find more information about the original goals of the projects here. For easier navigation, here is an index of the project descriptions in alphabetical order:

And now strap in, as there is a ton of great content to read about here!

Marcelo worked on improving the usability of cross-vendor GPU programs in Rust using the std::offload module. At the start of the project, the offload prototype was only a proof of concept. It assumed that the offloaded code was bug-free, and it required users to write a lot of boilerplate code. Marcelo resolved both issues over the summer.

First, he implemented proper type checking. Marcelo extended the compiler to verify that the arguments passed to any offload call are of the correct type, as expected by the GPU kernel. Kernel launches are thus now safe.

After that, he added support for generic kernels. The compiler now collects all generic instantiations launched from the CPU side, and loads that info later when compiling GPU kernels to make sure we instantiate them as needed. Marcelo also added support to select which GPU to use, which is helpful for laptops with both an integrated and a dedicated GPU, as well as for servers with multiple GPUs. He also added two macros that removed the need for any boilerplate when writing and launching GPU kernels.

The hardest part of this project by far was dealing with references. Due to Rust semantics, we cannot just map types containing mutable references to GPUs and then process them using multiple threads. Previous Rust GPU projects used raw pointers as a workaround, but we obviously wanted to avoid those. Marcelo managed to implement a sound abstraction so that users can now safely declare how their kernels will access mutable arguments.

As a cherry on top, Marcelo also ported the RajaPerf performance suite from C++ to Rust and used it to benchmark his pull requests. His safe Rust version matches the performance of the original C++ code, and is now described in a GPU offload paper that he is working on together with his mentor, Manuel. This was Marcelo's second Rust GSoC project, and same as last year, we are very happy with the results. Great job!

The goal of this project was simple on paper: teach the Wild linker to link WebAssembly (Wasm) programs. However, adding support for a new linker target is of course far from simple. Luckily, Kei already had a lot of experience with Wild, as this was his second GSoC project working on the Wild linker.

And as expected, Kei did a great job! Prior to GSoC 2026, Wild had no Wasm output support. Now, the Wasm support is sufficiently good that Wild can link a range of complex programs to Wasm. For example, it is able to link itself, SQLite, ripgrep, CPython and even the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine.

And the linking performance is excellent! When compared to wasm-ld, the de-facto standard Wasm linker, which is based on the LLD linker, Wild is 2-15x faster, and uses 2-5x less memory. You can find more benchmarks in his final report, where he also explains that achieving this performance took quite some work, because Wild's ELF linking performance did not immediately translate to being fast when linking Wasm.

Even after this GSoC project ended, Kei has continued improving Wild's Wasm support, as well as contributing to other parts of Wild. Thank you for bringing fast linking to a new set of use-cases, Kei! You are a valued member of the Wild team.

The goal of this project was to build the experimental std::autodiff module, which implements automatic differentiation of Rust code, and the std::offload module, which allows offloading Rust code to GPUs, in the CI of the Rust compiler.

Shota has already been contributing to this area in the months leading up to this year's GSoC, so he had no issues getting started. After valiantly fighting with our CI, he made both modules available in the official nightly compiler channel. Rust users can thus now simply install them with a single rustup command, rather than having to compile rustc from source! This is a huge benefit for gathering feedback on these features in the wild, as it makes it much easier to experiment with them.

Beyond making these projects available via rustup, he also worked on making it simpler to build projects that use std::offload. The original compilation pipeline was derived from Clang's support for GPU offload, so it involved calling clang helper binaries. That is clearly not optimal, so Shota worked on replacing it by directly calling the underlying LLVM APIs from rustc.

The last piece of his project was enabling testing in CI for both offload and autodiff, which already helped prevent multiple regressions. Right now, the GPU offload pipeline only tests the CPU setup side, but his work allowed us to talk to GPU hardware vendors, two of which already agreed to provide the Rust Project with GPU hardware so that in the future we can also run those tests on dedicated GPUs.

Overall, the project was a success. Shota had to show a lot of patience and endurance when working with various CMake quirks and CI challenges. We would like to extend a special thank you for that!

miri is a tool that can detect undefined behavior (UB) in unsafe Rust code. It used to have a prototype of an interactive debugger called priroda, but it became unmaintained some time ago. The goal of this project was to re-establish priroda, to make it easier to use miri interactively, debug how and why is UB introduced in Rust programs, and also help rustc developers analyse MIR, one of the intermediate representations of Rust programs.

Mohamed successfully reached both main goals of this project. He created a miri interface for the gdb debugger, which allows debugging programs executed by miri. You can set breakpoints, step through individual instructions, analyse MIR local variables and inspect the debugged program's state, with miri acting as a "virtual CPU". So when you encounter your next miri UB report, you can actually debug the program state that caused UB by running priroda! Mohamed also created a command-line interface for priroda, which is used to test it in miri's CI. This will ensure that it keeps working properly and will not bitrot again.

Mohamed also added basic support for the Debugger Adapter Protocol, which allows using priroda together with IDEs such as Visual Studio Code. Currently, connecting priroda to an IDE is a bit involved, so the next step would be to build a plugin for an IDE that would allow showing all the extra state that miri has, which gdb doesn't know how to interpret.

Debugging programs executed by miri is very exciting. Thank you for all your work!

The goal of this project was to implement two new language features that were accepted in RFC 3323:

Ryosuke had to familiarize himself with the compiler's codebase and do a lot of implementation work to get both features working. This included implementing parsing of the new syntax, recording its metadata in the compiler's Abstract Syntax Tree, implementing resolution of the restricted crate paths, and finally adding checks to enforce both restriction rules. This all amounted to around five thousand lines of Rust code!

Once the new features were implemented and available on nightly, Ryosuke wrote a Call for Testing blog post. It had to be very exciting to announce to the world that he implemented two new features from scratch, and people can now play with them on the nightly channel! After the blog post was published, users reported a few issues, which Ryosuke promptly fixed. He also contributed to rustdoc to improve how the impl and mut restrictions are rendered in the generated documentation pages.

Now that the features are available on nightly, feedback is being gathered on them, with the plan being to stabilize them in 2027. If you would like to provide feedback on the impl and mut restrictions, you can do so in this issue.

The goal of this project was clear, and Ryosuke achieved it completely. Awesome work!

The goal of this project, which was done in collaboration with the Rust Embedded Working Group, was to improve the API ergonomics and type safety of the serialport-rs crate.

The serialport project is a bit different from some other projects which participated in this year's Google Summer of Code. It is more on the side of "facility management" than rocket science. Its challenges are taming finicky operating system APIs and making good abstractions, rather than full-blown software engineering.

Tanmay led many fruitful discussions about potential design decisions, and did a lot of field research on how other crates that depend on serialport actually use its API, to figure out how to make the upcoming breaking API changes less disruptive and painful for them.

Tanmay also worked on sanding off some rough edges of the serialport API, such as replacing Boxed trait objects with enums, and making errors explicit in places where the legacy API used to panic. Some of the work still waits for integration. It is targeting the upcoming serialport 5.0 release.

Christian (Tanmay's mentor) found working alongside Tanmay very motivational, and he was able to catch up with a lot of other unrelated work in order to integrate Tanmay's changes. He noted that working with Tanmay was fun and productive, and that it was pure joy to see him grow from his first contribution in the bonding phase to seasoned contributions. Thank you, Tanmay!

This was my first Google Summer of Code as well. It was challenging, motivating, fun and definitely worth it. I would show up again.

libc is a foundational crate that is used by thousands of other crates across the Rust ecosystem. For the past several years, its maintainers have been attempting to publish a stable 1.0 release of the crate. Because this crate has to support interoperating with C on many compilation targets with weird quirks, this requires an enormous amount of work. We already had a GSoC project for moving libc towards 1.0 last year, and the goal of Adam's project was to make more progress in that direction.

And we can happily say that progress was indeed made! The original goal of Adam's project was to deprecate a number of constants that were difficult to maintain and cleanup inconsistencies in handling 32-bit/64-bit variants of file and time handling functions[2]. Adam was able to resolve that in a few weeks, and then he moved on to resolve a number of various issues blocking the 1.0 milestone.

Saying that Adam was productive would be… an understatement. We could follow his work in real-time, because he was posting daily GSoC reports for 116 days (!) in a row. The diligence and consistency with which he tackled so many complicated issues was an inspiration to us. In fact, sometimes the libc reviewers were not able to keep up!

You can find all Adam's libc pull requests here. You might notice that many of them have lots of comments, and even more discussions happened in GitHub issues and on Zulip. In addition to implementing the necessary code, making changes that affect interesting C platforms and architectures also required him to do a ton of research, and a lot of considerations of edge cases and possible backwards compatibility breakages. His work also took him on a whirlwind tour of diverse platforms; Adam's contributions spanned FreeBSD, NetBSD, Android, Hurd, NuttX, AIX, VxWorks, Fuchsia, L4Re and more.

Even though more work will still be required to get libc to 1.0, Adam's contributions made a significant dent in this effort. Thank you very much for all your work!

Linker scripts are arcane commands that can be used to instruct a linker to construct the final binary in a custom way. The Wild linker used to implement only basic linker script functionality, which Vishruth greatly expanded during his GSoC project.

Thanks to that, Wild can now successfully link Linux kernel modules, and it's even close to being able to link the Linux kernel itself! Vishruth's work involved greatly expanding expression evaluation support, location counters, program headers, etc. In addition to adding support for many missing bits of linker script support, Vishruth implemented support for partial linking (-r) as this is needed in order to link Linux kernel modules. You can find all the linker script features that he implemented here.

Adding all those peculiar features to Wild required performing many cross-cutting changes to its codebase, which Vishruth managed to do really well. And it was not at the cost of performance! Wild now manages to link Linux kernel modules such as btrfs or amdgpu 2-4x faster than the BFD (GNU ld) or LLD linkers[3]. You can find more benchmarks in his final report.

Vishruth has continued to contribute to Wild even after his GSoC project ended and has become a valued contributor to the project. Thank you very much for making Wild better, Vishruth!

rust-analyzer uses rowan for its syntax trees, a library for Concrete Syntax Trees. rowan has served us well over the years, but it has some downsides that cause major performance problems and also smaller convenience issues. In particular, memory fragmentation causes rust-analyzer to consume much more memory than it actually needs (in the order of redundant gigabytes).

We wanted to rewrite rowan to change that. The problem was that many parts in rust-analyzer touch syntax trees, and in particular assists (code actions) of which we have a lot. They also use mutable tree editing, a feature of rowan that can be convenient but was a major obstacle in rewriting it to be more efficient.

During his project, bit-aloo first migrated all rust-analyzer code from mutable tree editing to SyntaxEditor, a new abstraction that was created specifically to avoid mutation. After that, he removed mutable editing from rowan altogether.

The migration process is incremental and rowan is still inefficient in various aspects. However, we believe that the parts which required changes to large amounts of code are behind us, and we can complete the migration with more focused changes. bit-aloo is continuing to work on that even after his GSoC project ended. And he was also accepted as a member of the rust-analyzer team, so congratulations! We would like to thank him for his work, and hope to continue working with him to improve rust-analyzer for everyone.

The std::arch module of the Rust standard library contains various intrinsic functions that provide architecture and vendor-specific functionality. Their implementation lives in the stdarch repository, which is included as a Josh subtree in the main compiler repo (rust-lang/rust).

When someone changes the intrinsics in the main repo, breakages can silently creep in, because the main repo does not execute all the stdarch tests in its CI. That can cause friction when we synchronize the changes between the two repositories. Ideally, we would run all of stdarch's tests in the main repo to detect any issues as soon as possible.

And that is where Sumit came in! Over the course of his GSoC project, he examined the (very!) complex ways the intrinsics are tested in stdarch, and started porting them over to the main repo. But this was not a matter of copying over a few lines of YAML. The compiler repo uses its own build system (called bootstrap) and a CI workflow structure that is quite different from the stdarch repository. Sumit thus had to first understand what is each test suite doing, reimplement it as a part of bootstrap and finally integrate it into the compiler's CI workflows.

We run ~90 CI jobs across several hardware architectures, operating systems and OS versions. Getting all that to work while testing vendor-specific intrinsics required a lot of diligent work… and a lot of patience. It took five months for one of the test suites to finally succeed on the main repo's CI, and it required Sumit to completely refactor how the suite worked, for it to be more compatible with bootstrap. As another example, a different test suite that Sumit also got to work required running the tests in an Intel CPU emulator on CI.

Sumit ported most of the stdarch test suites to bootstrap, including intrinsics verification against reference C implementations, checks for automatically generated source code being up-to-date, and various unit tests for individual intrinsics and CPU feature detection logic. There is one remaining test suite to port, but the ported tests are already helping us find issues, which is great.

You can check Sumit's rust-lang PRs here; notice that he was also contributing to other parts of Rust in the meantime! Sumit's work will help us make LLVM upgrades and land intrinsics changes more easily. Thank you, Sumit!

The goal of this project was to get rid of a very scary place in the Rust compiler's test suite: a directory called tests/ui/issues. It contained thousands of test files based on historical Rust issues, dating back all the way to 2012. The problem with those tests was that they were named only with an issue number (e.g. issue-37291). When such a test would break, it was quite difficult to figure out what was it even supposed to test, because there was little context attached to it.

Even though we already had a GSoC project to tackle this problem last year, due to the sheer amount of uncategorized tests, there were still over four hundred tests left in this directory by the time zedddie started working on this project.

For each test in this directory, zedddie had to first understand what was the test doing and dig through its original GitHub issue and any other related issues and pull requests. Then they had to figure out what would be the best location to move the test under, search for any possible duplicates, come up with a descriptive name for the test (that tends to be very difficult!), and finally add a short description to the test that explains the context of why the test was added in the first place. Rinse and repeat, for hundreds of tests.

zedddie rolled up their sleeves, and categorized over 300 tests in 30 pull requests. Together with other contributors helping out over this summer, zedddie was finally able to remove the last batch of uncategorized tests at the start of August. As zedddie said in their final report: "What is left to do: nothing, tests/ui/issues is gone".

While this work might sound a bit bland, its positive effect on the maintainability of our test suite, and improving the lives of Rust compiler contributors, is considerable. It is also apparently a great way to learn about cool niche edge cases of Rust that most Rust developers might not know about! After migrating the remaining uncategorized UI tests, zedddie continued contributing to the next trait solver and const generics. Thank you very much for helping us finally get rid of tests/ui/issues, zedddie!

The Rust debugging experience leaves a lot to be desired. One reason why we struggled to improve it is that many of our debuginfo test suites did not even run in CI for the past few years, as they were difficult to maintain. When something changed in the type visualizers, the implementation details of a standard library type or in debugger internals, someone had to go through tens of tests and manually update them. This was not sustainable, so the test suite rotted.

Luckily for us, Anthony took that affront personally. Even before his GSoC project, he spent considerable effort on improving the quality of debug visualizers of various Rust standard library types, and gained an impressive amount of knowledge about debuggers.

During his GSoC project, he completely overhauled how our debuginfo test infrastructure works, both for LLDB and GDB. Thanks to his improvements, we can now easily "rebless" the reference output when something changes, which makes it much easier to keep our test suite up-to-date. The new tests also record much more information about the internal state of the debugger recorded during the test, which helps with diagnosing issues that cause type visualizers to stop working.

In addition to redesigning the test suite, Anthony also actually managed to re-enable the LLDB tests on both Windows and Linux in our CI again (after several years of being skipped there!). This will allow us to avoid debuginfo regressions and make it easier to improve the Rust debugging experience. Oh, and it goes without saying that while doing all that, he also made numerous improvements to Rust type visualizers. You can find his PRs here.

Anthony's amazing contributions and his deep expertise in debuggers led to him being invited to the Rust Compiler team, which was much deserved. What else can we add, other than: thank you for your awesome work!

The support for platform-specific directories (platformdirs) has been a long-standing feature request for rustup, to have more fine-grained filesystem directory choices. This project investigated how that issue could be resolved.

The real complexity of this feature request lies within a decade worth of different assumptions that previous iterations of rustup and cargo have made: it turns out that quite a lot of them are no longer true if we were to implement platformdirs support truly faithfully.

Guicheng first worked on cleaning up the interactions between rustup self uninstall and $CARGO_HOME/bin as a warmup. This issue itself is a very good demonstration of all that compatibility baggage: somehow $CARGO_HOME/bin has become the default binary directory for all things Rust, so rustup ended up installing itself and all its proxies into it. As a result, it has been super annoying to many that everything in $CARGO_HOME is gone with rustup self uninstall.

After that, he started the actual implementation of platformdirs support in rustup. This was no easy task! Not because the code itself was hard to write, but because it takes a lot of effort to figure out what should be the desired behavior in the first place. Also, in order to determine the appropriate platformdirs semantics, some prior research is often required to see how things became what they are today, so the decoupling of different concerns could proceed, and migration paths could be designed accordingly. It was in this sense that this is different from a typical GSoC project, and luckily thanks to the effort he has put into this project, we have not only come up with the final patch, but also discovered and fixed some tiny preexisting issues with this long-untouched aspect of the rustup codebase along the way.

Thank you for digging into this complex topic, Guicheng!

We would like to thank all contributors who have participated in Google Summer of Code 2026 with us! Your contributions helped make Rust better, and introduced you as new members of our community, which is a reason to celebrate. We are looking forward to participating in GSoC again next year!

We would also like to thank Google for organizing the Google Summer of Code program and for allowing us to host a large number of projects every year. And last, but not least, we would like to thank all the Rust mentors who were tirelessly helping our contributors to complete their projects. Without you, Rust GSoC would not be possible.

97.5% over a three-year period, if you are wondering (40 out of 41 projects were successful so far). ↩

If you were wondering, then yes, this is actually related to the famous 2038 problem :) ↩

In case you were wondering, the mold linker does not support linker scripts required to link Linux kernel modules at the moment, so Vishruth did not compare the performance of Wild against mold here. ↩

#9934. Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image

The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong.

This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data.

The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica.

Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape.

Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error.

To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today.

In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said.

He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image.

"Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said.

Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

#9933. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

#9932. Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Attackers can exploit a flaw in Claude's document-processing tool by creating a temporary file that Anthropic's AI assistant can access and run on a user's machine.

An attacker can use a flaw in Anthropic Claude's document-processing tool to run malicious code on Linux systems just by creating a temporary file that the AI assistant can access. The flaw highlights a growing risk posed by even trusted AI tools to introduce security gaps in enterprise environments.

Researchers from AIR Security discovered the flaw, which they've dubbed "Office Party," in Anthropic's official DOCX, PPTX, and XLSX skills, which are tools that enable Claude to create, read, edit, and process Microsoft Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and Excel spreadsheets, respectively.

The vulnerability stems from a helper script, soffice.py, that launches LibreOffice to convert documents, including rendering Word documents as PDFs, they revealed in a report published today. When the script encounters an environment where Unix-domain sockets cannot be opened, it uses a workaround that loads a shared library through the Linux LD_PRELOAD mechanism.

Related:N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

Anthropic has opted not to fix the issue.

During conversation, the script checks whether a library named lo_socket_shim.so already exists in a shared temporary directory but does not verify its origin or contents. An attacker who can place a malicious library at that location before the next document-processing operation can potentially have their code loaded and executed within LibreOffice, with the privileges of the user running the AI agent.

In this way, the flaw can allow attackers to execute malicious code on a user's Linux machine by exploiting an unverified file path used during document conversion, explains Niv Hoffman, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of AIR Research Lab, in an email interview.

"An attacker gets one malicious file into a shared temporary folder which many programs use, and the next time an employee asks Claude for a document, Anthropic's trusted skill loads that file and runs it," he tells Dark Reading.

The vulnerability affects Linux environments where Unix sockets are blocked, including certain container security configurations, and Claude Code's sandbox. AIR Security reports that macOS is not affected because it does not load the library through LD_PRELOAD.

The AIR researchers demonstrated two ways the attack can work on Linux systems. In one scenario, they manually placed a malicious library in the temporary directory before asking Claude Code to generate a document. In another, they used a separate, seemingly legitimate AI skill to unpack a supporting file into the same directory. When the document-processing skill subsequently ran, the malicious library was loaded automatically.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The flaw presents a serious issue for enterprises running Linux because it exploits "the default skills that all Claude agents use — [of which there are] hundreds of millions — and one planted file can make them run an attacker’s code with the employee's own access," Hoffman explains.

This second attack scenario is particularly concerning for enterprise security teams because it illustrates how individually benign-looking AI skills can interact to create an attack chain. And often, "companies don't have visibility to which skills and other agent add-ons they have installed, and don't have a red button to revoke or patch a vulnerable one," Hoffman explains.

Moreover, a malicious or compromised skill does not necessarily need to exploit the document-processing tool directly; it may simply need to place a file that another trusted component will execute, according to the AIR researchers.

The AIR team discovered the flaw in May and reported it to Anthropic, which acknowledged its existence, according to the report. However, the AI company "considers it outside its security boundary, since the vulnerable code only runs inside a sandbox," AIR Research Lab's Omri Saxena and Or Nevo wrote in the report. This means that as of now, the helper script still uses the same fixed path and still loads whatever file it finds there, they said.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Hoffman says that Anthropic's response is "not quite" adequate, "because even if the skills run within a sandbox, the attacker’s code then runs inside it with the user's own permissions, where the user's files and work already are," he says. Anthropic did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment about whether the company would take any further action to remedy the issue.

For businesses deploying AI agents and coding assistants, Office Party reinforces the need to treat AI skills as software dependencies rather than trusted extensions, and secure them as such, according to AIR.

To mitigate, organizations should make it a point to know "exactly what skills or add-ons an organization is using with Claude Code by keeping a live inventory of every AI skill and add-on across employees' agents," Hoffman says. They also should "review even official ones like any other code, and update or patch the whole set whenever a new vulnerability is published."
