#9884. Lock your GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions now supports workflow lockfiles.

Because GitHub Actions are fetched from Git, the previous advice was to pin to a full SHA instead of a tag. This is because tags are mutable and susceptible to supply-chain attacks where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code.

Install the gh-actions-lock extension to the gh CLI:

The workflow now uses vX.Y.Z tags and looks like this:

And it generates a lockfile at .github/workflows/actions.lock:

Commit modified workflows and the new lockfile.

Good news, both already support lockfiles! Your periodic updates will also update the lockfile. Remember to use cooldowns.

GitHub also recommends verifying lockfiles in CI to ensure it’s up-to-date and not corrupt.

They suggest copying this verify-lockfile.yml into your repo. I decided to put it into my existing lint workflow, but in its own job so it runs independently and in parallel:

Note I’m using the lightweight ubuntu-slim runner here. Also, it’s pinning to v0.4.1; we’ll have to update that at some point or figure out a way to automate it. That’s for another time.

Don’t forget that we just modified the actions in a workflow, so need to relock with gh actions-lock. Nothing actually changes if adding to lint.yml because it’s already locking actions/checkout. But if you created a new file like verify-lockfile.yml, you’ll need to relock for that. The CI will let you know.

zizmor is a security linter for GitHub Actions and strongly recommended. If you don’t use it, please do.

Versions before v1.32.0 tell you to hash-pin actions, and v1.32.0 is the first to support lockfiles.

I use zizmor in prek, so add/update zizmor in .pre-commit-config.yaml:

#9883. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

#9881. .name grandfathered

After a long and expensive battle, news just dropped that Verisign is retracting its plan to terminate 22,000 domain names and email redirects. Although they will be closing new registrations for 3rd-level .name domains, all existing domains (including this website) and email redirects will remain indefinitely.

This was a team effort. It was inspiring how many talented people joined this fight. From Doytchin who kicked everything off, to Jim who flew to Bali to make the case to ICANN in person, to Patrik, Troy, Huyen, Keith, Judy, Erik, and Ryan who wrote formal reconsideration requests, to my lawyers Jan, Flip and Diégo who threw the book at ICANN, to Beverly, Stefan, Vaughan, Irv, Pablo, Larry, Lionel, Daniel, Ori, Markus, Kirk, Ed, Jeremy, Stephan, Matija, Jan, Simon, Mark, and Evan who filed letters of support. I'd also like to sincerely thank selected individuals within ICANN who had the courage to stand up against the bureaucracy. Without exception, everyone I spoke with was a remarkable person.

InfoQ Homepage Articles The iOS Crash We Could Not Reproduce

Nov 11, 2026 10 min read

Some production crashes announce themselves with a clean stack trace. This one did not. It appeared in a large-scale consumer iOS application, affected only some executions, and resisted every local reproduction attempt. The final code change was small, but reaching it required turning a vague SIGBUS report into a controlled set of experiments. This article walks through the investigation and the threading contract behind HTML import in NSAttributedString.

Most production crashes I investigate start with a familiar routine. I read the crash report, look for the stack frame closest to the failure, try to reproduce the path, and then work backward toward the root cause. This incident did not fit that pattern.

The crash showed up in a large-scale consumer iOS application. It affected only a subset of executions and appeared at unpredictable times. Exact production metrics are confidential, but the incident was serious enough to require a focused investigation and an expedited hotfix.

Neither developers nor QA engineers could reproduce it consistently. We could repeat the customer flow without seeing anything unusual. The crash report included a SIGBUS signal and Foundation frames related to attributed string processing, but it did not point to a clear line in our Swift code.

SIGBUS is a low-level invalid memory access signal, not a diagnosis. It can come from several conditions, so it would have been wrong to assume from the signal alone that a specific variable had been released or reused. The evidence narrowed the search area, but it did not establish the cause.

That left a wide search space. I considered object lifetime, SwiftUI view model ownership, shared mutable state, unsynchronized work, and Foundation behavior. Management needed an answer quickly, and I initially had about a week to investigate and prepare a fix.

I started with the checks that usually help with this kind of failure. I enabled Zombie Objects, added exception and symbolic breakpoints, reviewed ownership around the affected screens, and inspected the asynchronous paths that prepared their data.

I also made defensive improvements while I was in that part of the codebase. I tightened observable object ownership, reviewed whether several reference types really needed identity semantics, clarified synchronization, and made UI-related concurrency more explicit with async and await and MainActor isolation.

Those changes improved the code. The first hotfix also produced a noticeable reduction in the overall crash rate. But the original crash signature continued to appear in production, and customers were still reporting the behavior tied to the incident.

The initial improvement looked encouraging because the aggregate crash rate moved in the right direction. It did not prove causation. Changes to lifecycle handling and synchronization can affect task scheduling, object retention, and timing. A timing-sensitive failure can become less frequent even when the underlying contract violation is still present.

That distinction became central to the investigation. We had improved the application, but we had not shown that we had removed the defect. The target crash still existed, and the remaining investigation window had narrowed to only a few days.

The turning point was not another breakpoint or a more detailed stack trace. A QA engineer who also used the production application found that she could trigger the crash by repeating the affected flow. It was still intermittent and sometimes took four or five attempts, but that was enough.

For the first time, I had a practical test oracle. If a new build still crashed on that device, the change had not addressed the problem. If repeated attempts stopped producing the failure, the change deserved deeper validation. The device changed the work from production forensics into an experiment.

My first experiments still focused on the screens closest to the visible failure. I cleaned up their code, adjusted ownership, reviewed asynchronous work, generated an IPA, and sent it to the QA engineer.

After several attempts, that build crashed again. The result was negative, but it was useful. Until then, I had been making reasonable changes without a reliable way to know whether they mattered. A reproducible failure made every rejected hypothesis informative.

The loop became simple: change one area, build an IPA, install it on the affected device, repeat the customer flow, and record whether the crash returned. Across the investigation, I shared roughly nine or ten experimental builds.

I also explored potential solutions through developer communities, including Stack Overflow, the Apple Developer Forums, and LinkedIn iOS development groups. However, the application's source code and internal debugging artifacts were confidential under company policies, so I could only discuss the problem at a general technical level without sharing proprietary information. While these communities offered opportunities to explore possible causes, they could not directly inspect or conclusively diagnose the issue. I therefore continued investigating through controlled experiments within our development environment.

I changed the question. Instead of asking which code looked suspicious, I asked which code had to remain for the crash to survive. I removed one view or behavior at a time, generated a new build, and tested the same flow on the affected device.

After six or seven elimination builds, the failure surface narrowed to one file. Nothing in that file looked obviously unsafe, so I repeated the process inside it. Several more experiments reduced the problem to one operation.

The line converted HTML data into an attributed string:

The code had no force unwrap, unsafe pointer, manual memory management, or obvious shared state. At the call site, it looked like a normal Foundation conversion. That ordinary appearance had kept it low on the original list of suspects.

The affected flow involved two important views of the application. Each view displayed a static disclosure section near the bottom, containing legal and informational text formatted as HTML. Although the content itself was static, it included interactive elements such as hyperlinks and phone numbers that users could tap to open external web views or initiate phone calls.

The application received this disclosure content as HTML and converted it into an attributed string before rendering it on the screen.

Because the disclosure section was relatively small and worked correctly during most executions, it initially appeared unlikely to be responsible for the crash. Attention naturally focused on the larger architectural components and asynchronous screen-loading operations.

The critical issue was that HTML-to-attributed-string conversion could be invoked from an asynchronous screen-preparation path without an explicit guarantee of main-thread execution. This mattered because Foundation's HTML importer has a threading constraint that was not enforced at the call site.

Apple documents an important constraint for HTML import through NSAttributedString: when the options specify HTML as the document type, the importer should not be called from a background thread. Apple says the method may try to synchronize with the main thread, fail, and time out. The broader attributed string documentation also notes that WebKit handles HTML conversion, which matters because this path is not just a pure data transformation.

Our problem was therefore not that the screens displayed attributed text. The unsafe condition came from creating HTML-backed attributed strings from an execution context where the main thread was not guaranteed.

The API did not make that requirement obvious at the call site. It accepted a Data value and returned an attributed string, so it looked like a straightforward transformation. The implementation carried a platform constraint that the surrounding asynchronous architecture had to enforce.

Timing-dependent defects can survive many successful executions. Two users may receive equivalent HTML and call the same Swift function, yet reach the importer under different scheduling conditions. One execution may occur safely while another reaches the same code from background work during screen preparation.

This also explained why the defensive hotfix reduced the observed frequency without removing the signature. Lifecycle and synchronization changes changed timing. They did not eliminate the unsupported execution context.

The practical lesson was clear: changing the probability of a concurrency failure is not the same as removing its cause. For this incident to be considered resolved, the targeted crash signature and the reproducing flow both had to confirm the fix.

The immediate repair was to perform the HTML conversion on the main actor. Fixing only the original call site would have addressed the visible incident, but it would not have prevented the same mistake elsewhere in a large codebase.

I searched for every place where the application converted HTML into an attributed string. Then I introduced a shared helper that made the execution requirement part of the API instead of an instruction each developer had to remember. The following code is a simplified and anonymized representation of that design:

The UI-facing caller also stayed isolated to the main actor:

Existing call sites were routed through this helper. The design centralized the Foundation dependency, reduced duplication, and created one place to document and test the threading contract. More importantly, it turned the requirement from a convention into a code-level boundary.

This did not mean all screen preparation moved to the main actor. Networking, decoding, and other suitable work could remain asynchronous. Only the operation with the framework constraint, along with the UI state that consumed its result, needed explicit main-actor isolation.

I sent the corrected build to the QA engineer and asked her to repeat the flow on the device that had exposed every earlier attempt. The failure no longer appeared. I then asked for additional testing across both affected views and nearby behavior before promoting the change to the hotfix branch.

After release, production monitoring showed a dramatic reduction in the targeted crash. Exact figures cannot be disclosed, but this outcome differed from the first hotfix in the way that mattered: the specific production signature no longer appeared at a meaningful rate.

The investigation ended with three validations rather than one. The known device stopped reproducing the issue, every related call site used the shared helper, and production monitoring confirmed the expected change.

The most useful lesson was broader than one Foundation API. When evidence is incomplete, a debugging process has to create new evidence. A device that reproduced the crash intermittently was more valuable than a long list of plausible code changes because it allowed each hypothesis to fail clearly.

The incident also changed how I evaluate framework abstractions. A Swift initializer may look safe while hiding behavior inherited from Objective-C, Foundation, UIKit, WebKit, run loops, or older platform design. Swift concurrency makes execution context easier to express, but it does not automatically make every underlying API safe for concurrent use.

Finally, a successful repair should make the same defect harder to reintroduce. The shared helper mattered because it protected future call sites, not only the two views involved in the incident.

The final code change was small. The hard part was reaching it through incomplete crash information, an unreproducible flow, misleading early improvements, time pressure, and proprietary artifacts that could not be shared outside the organization.

Once a single device reproduced the failure, the investigation stopped depending on intuition. Repeated builds narrowed the problem from two screens to one file and then to one ordinary-looking Foundation call. The root cause was HTML import running without the main-thread guarantee required by its implementation.

When a stack trace cannot identify the bug, the next step is to design an experiment that forces the code to reveal it. In this incident, systematic fault isolation provided the evidence that ordinary debugging could not.

#9879. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9878. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9876. For the first time, a C++ standard failed to pass the national bodies

Local 'minimal viable product that everyone agrees on' tanks the C++ standard.

It looks like it happened! A historic first, for better or worse.

This is a sign that C++ is (still) struggling with its governance (see a previous article on cultural issues within C++ here). This is a big deal even if you do not care about programming languages. C++ is arguably the most important programming language in existence.

Your computer runs on C or C++. The web browser you are using to read this is written in C++. ~All programming languages depend on C++ (often through LLVM). Likewise, ~all websites with performance requirements (e.g. YouTube) depend on C++, ~all data storage, game engines, finance, etc.

In a world that is drowning in exciting new vulnerabilities in ~all software, the ability of C++ to change and adjust to changing times affects you.

Let’s take a step back and get an overview. The initial source was a post by Robert Seacord on LinkedIn:

In a comment, J. Daniel GarcÃ­a adds: “There were 12 countries that abstained. In several cases because they could not reach to a common position. That is another signal of a contested draft.”

Now, before we get into the facts: This is not a good look for C++.

There have been multiple fights over the future direction of the C++ language, but no C++ standard ever failed to be signed off by the national bodies.

The national body vote is considered to be a formality. By the time the vote reaches the national bodies all disagreements should’ve been sorted out by WG21 (Working Group 21, i.e. the C++ Standards Committee).

Truly controversial features should never make it this far, since they should never be added to the C++26 working draft in the first place. This is a sign of division in the C++ community, in some form or another, and completely independently of whether you agree with this result or not.

Here, “Added to the C++26 working draft” is essentially accepting the pull request. Everyone is working towards the C++26 release, and people contribute to it with papers. Papers lead to votes, which then lead to amendments of the draft. Finally (this is where we are) wording passes happen, and it gets signed off, rubber-stamped and released. Phrased like this, the ISO process sounds sensible enough, but trust me, it’s actually kind of a nightmare.

Needless to say, the debates are raging, with comments on all sides: So many discussions.

Quick explanation: The national bodies execute a single vote. To pass the national bodies, the draft has to meet two bars:

If the above posts are correct, then the draft failed to meet both bars. Twelve isn’t two-thirds of twenty, and nine is more than a quarter. Visualization:

In total, there were 20 P-members, and 22 total members (ignoring abstaining). I heard that the US abstained, but take that with a grain of salt.

tl;dr: WG21 voted to include Contracts in C++26. Several high-ranking members of WG21 are strongly opposed to Contracts, and so are several national bodies. The national body vote was the ’last resort’ place to prevent Contracts from being canonicalized as part of the C++ standard.

New keywords that replace assert macros with a standardized way to enforce runtime checks. Most importantly, you can add pre and post checks to ensure that all arguments and return values fulfill certain conditions.

Looks simple, right? You’d think so, but no!

First, due to issues with virtual functions, Contracts for virtual functions were already cut from the proposal.

Second, it’s not entirely obvious how this will interact with constexpr or function inlining.

Third, there are compile flags to selectively enable or disable the enforcement. E.g. “If a contract is violated, do you want to 1) kill the program, 2) call a ‘contract-violation handler’ and then kill the program, 3) log an error, 4) ignore completely (and not even perform the check, for performance reasons)?”

Big question: You compile your code with enforce and are linking a prebuilt library that pulls in the same dependency as you, but with Contracts set to ignore. This is fine according to Contracts. The linker gets to keep one of the copies. What happens? Do Contracts run or not? What if a call is inlined across translation units?

Is there even a way for the user to guarantee that checks always run? (The answer is no. What? You were hoping that this feature could be used to ensure certain checks guarding against Undefined Behavior would always run, no matter what? Don’t be silly—this is C++.)

Oh, did I mention that code inside of predicates is just standard C++, so the compiler is allowed to elide checks due to Undefined Behavior?

But do feel free to take it from the source: The “Contracts paper” can be found here, and if you read closely, you’ll find some funny statements that really ruffled some feathers:

It is ill-formed, no diagnostic required (IFNDR) if multiple first declarations for the same function are in different translation units that do not have the same sequence of function contract specifiers.

All of this leads to so many funny issues, some of which can be poorly summarized as “Well, who even knows whether your Contracts are even going to be enforced, this is C++, the compiler can do whatever it wants lol”.

If you think “Gee, this proposal looks rather complex and messy”, keep in mind that the Contracts paper was explicitly designed to be a minimal viable product that everyone would be able to agree on.

If you only faintly paid attention to C++, you might be going into this assuming that Profiles (aka Bjarne Stroustrup’s initiative to make C++ safer via magical fairy dust, also controversial and considered to be ‘impossible to implement’ by some) are the sticking point, but no, Profiles did not make it into C++26.

Oh, y’know, it’s just because that’s all everyone has been talking about.

Most obviously, the pro-Contracts camp released “Do not remove Contracts from C++26” on Oct 23rd, i.e. around the time when the national body ballot closed. Vinnie Falco (the most outspoken voice against Contracts) countered with “Do Remove Contracts From C++26” on the very same day1.

If you’ve been paying attention, there’s a whole trail of papers and events here.

We’ve got talks, and Bjarne Stroustrup, the creator of C++ himself, saying “it’s claimed to be a minimum viable product. It is not minimal. I don’t think it’s viable”.

We’ve got multiple papers, say “Contract Concerns”, “Contracts make C++ less safe — full stop!”, or “Contracts’ fundamental flaws” (all reasonably short) opposing the behemoth that’s the Contracts paper and its rationale document (put together, almost 300 pages).

We’ve had multiple votes. Most importantly (Hagenberg, Feb 15th, 2025), the vote to formally add Contracts to the C++26 working draft, turned out 100 in favor, 14 opposed, 12 abstain. The multiple votes to remove Contracts from the draft all failed, most recently in Croydon, which is also when an amendment to support a mechanism to ensure mandatory contract enforcement failed.

If your eyes are glazing over at this point, I don’t blame you!

The whole situation is a mess, and trying to keep track of it from the outside is a fool’s errand: You’re basically forced to track dry meeting notes, and read between the lines looking at the various drafts people are publishing. Don’t do it.

This is not Contracts’ first rodeo: A different version of Contracts was up for debate around 2018, and was kicked out not too long after. At this point SG21 (‘Study Group 21’) was formed, dedicated to revamping the Contracts concept to get us the new “Minimum Viable Product” that’s currently part of the draft.

The whole situation went back and forth, resulted in fourteen revisions on the Contracts paper, many comments from the national bodies during the process, and finally in some people explicitly calling for the national bodies to veto C++26. (We call that ’the nuclear option’. FYI, some of the people signing this are themselves sitting on national bodies.)

What you need to understand is that the Hagenberg vote (on adding Contracts to the working draft) was strongly in favor of Contracts. 100 in favor vs. 14 against is not a weak result. This makes it incredibly puzzling that this final vote failed so badly (12 for, 8 against is bad).

One narrative on what happened is the following:

“There’s a loud minority strongly opposing Contracts in C++26. This group includes people with a lot of influence, e.g. Bjarne Stroustrup. Some members of this group actively lobbied the national bodies to vote against Contracts, even though WG21 achieved alignment, and agrees that Contracts should ship in their current form.”

This agrees with the evidence we’ve seen (votes in favor, some people strongly opposed). Herb Sutter is suggesting this in his latest paper, see here. (Herb Sutter, for the record, was the chair of the C++ Committee and is (next to Bjarne) perhaps the second-most-important person anyone in the C++ world listens to.)

This is plausible, but I don’t believe it. Not entirely, anyway. Yes, lobbying happened, and Bjarne’s opinion is something people listen to. It’s possible it was the deciding factor, but if it was the deciding factor, then this is a sign that the process itself is broken, and puts undue value onto status.

Even Herb Sutter acknowledges that Contracts were contentious. In footnote 4 on his paper, anyway.

Some of the NBs that voted Disapprove had participated and had expressed concerns about contracts without having to be lobbied (importantly, those were the first-ever Disapprove votes on any C++ DIS).

In other words, before any lobbying happened we already had a historical first, the strongest ever NB disagreement with a draft.

Importantly, it looks to me as though the committee just repeatedly ignored the comments/feedback of the national bodies throughout the process, and then ran face-first into a wall at the vote.

If you think “Oh, you are saying that the committee is just straight-up incompetent and/or evil, then?” No, not really. The committee process is just such a mess that it semi-naturally leads to situations like this. The people working within this system have become so used to the process that they’re barely capable of seeing it.

(Over the years many people who did not find this process workable just left entirely. There’s a huge selection bias effect.)

Part of what makes the process bad is that it’s very “all or nothing”, and the process is so slow that working on the standard is painful for everyone. More on that later.

Anyway. I don’t believe that it’s all just the lobbying. The discussions were already way underway. Evidence:

Taking a look at “Do not remove Contracts from C++26”, it refers to the “23 NB comments on contract assertions”.

Taking a closer look at N5028 and N5031, we see the committee rejected at least one strong anti-Contracts comment from each of the following countries: Sweden, Spain, the United States, France, Romania, the Czech Republic and Finland.

These comments included multiple asks to not ship Contracts in their current form at all, resolve safety issues, make Contracts reliably non-ignorable, fix the const issues, and change it such that standard library hardening phrasing does not depend on Contracts.

What did the committee think? That all of these asks were completely irrelevant? Yeah, no shit people are going to vote against something or abstain if you ignore their concerns.

This was preventable! People told you ahead of time that they were strongly opposed! The national bodies played their part correctly here. They gave you feedback ahead of time, and then voted accordingly.

There were at least four comments asking specifically “Please do not make the work on ‘standard library hardening’ depend on the inclusion of Contracts into C++26.” As it stands, this coupling is still there, i.e. the comments were ignored.

In fact, now that the future of Contracts is shaky, the “Do not remove Contracts” paper includes the following line:

At the time of writing, there is no wording for removing contract assertions from C++26, and producing it is not a purely mechanical exercise. It would require:

removing or respecifying C++26 standard-library hardening [P3471R4], which is written in terms of contract assertions and has never had complete, reviewed wording that is independent of contract assertions.

The audacity. The national bodies were very explicit in saying that they do not want standard library hardening to depend on Contracts.

You went and ignored those comments, and are now complaining about the effort that would be necessary to walk things back? You were given all the heads-up you needed, you just ignored it!

I quote Footnote 6 from Herb Sutter’s paper on the situation we are in. If there is an expert, it is him:

P3911 is the only technical proposal that NBs told us during CD comment processing would likely prevent multiple potential NB negative votes. Itâs also a pure extension that doesnât disturb the rest of the contracts design or interfere with future extensions, which makes it low-cost and low-risk to adopt. This is why in Kona I repeatedly encouraged EWG to pursue it. It addresses what several experts said was their principal concern motivated by safety issues: to provide a way to write a contract in source code that would be guaranteed to be enforced at execution time regardless of build mode or linking. However, it failed to be approved in the EWG 2026-01 telecon (âencourage more work in this directionâ failed by 8-25 for-against, with 9 neutral). Now we have the new information that NBs have rejected the DIS, and several have again cited safety as a critical issue, so this change is likely to increase NB consensus.

P3911 is the paper that proposes adding a way to ensure Contracts will always run, and can be enforced.

(Which, yes, a lot of people believe is necessary for a safety feature. If you can’t guarantee the safety is even enforced, what’s the point?)

Honestly, probably not. Herb Sutter is looking at the situaation from the political angle, and analyzing whose beliefs have more weight based on their status.

Bjarne Stroustrup’s beliefs (as the creator of C++) hold a lot of weight. This is correct.

Quoting Herb Sutter’s discussion on the matter:

Over half of the NBs that voted Disapprove on the C++26 DIS had never participated in WG21 at all and/or never before expressed any concern about contracts in C++26 (most sent no comments on the C++26 CD comment ballot; one sent contracts-unrelated CD comments), yet voted against the DIS after being lobbied with messages citing Bjarneâs opposition.

“Look! It’s just Bjarne having a lot of status!” he says, and he is completely right in saying so, but he is also acting as though putting huge pressure on members to “disagree and commit :-)” hadn’t always been part of it. The C++ Standards Committee always voted in terms of factions.

It was always a political mess where Bjarne’s explicit support was absolutely critical, and where “I know you may disagree with this, but you should vote in favor to get it in” was a part of the process.

Quoting Herb Sutter and Bjarne, yet again from Herb Sutter’s paper:

(Ed.: Bjarne added, when reviewing this paper, that one reason previous DIS ballots were unanimous was his private and public encouragement.)

Why are Contracts authors so obsessed with getting Contracts into C++26? Why not wait for the next release?

Well, C++ has this funny “release train model” (also known as “the frame rule bus stop analogy” in Super Mario Bros. speedrunning). A new version of the C++ standard releases every three years. If your work gets voted into the standard in time, it becomes part of it. If it doesn’t, you have to wait another three years for the next release.

Three years is a long time, and it’s an especially long time to work on a single C++ feature. Getting a C++ paper accepted into the standard is a process so notoriously draining that ~all of the “C++ people” I know just stopped bothering, and stopped working with WG21. It’s bad.

If Contracts don’t get in this cycle, there’s a good chance they never will. They will be nitpicked over the next three years, endlessly litigated, and frankly, I think there’s a good chance several of the people working on Contracts just won’t want to deal with that, and might instead drop out of the process entirely, leaving Contracts dead and buried.

Until the process itself changes, which, god knows how that could happen considering the requirements presumably imposed by ISO, it’s hard to imagine this changing.

This is why the pro-Contracts side released the following statement in their paper:

If the DIS ballot has failed, we should seek another ballot without altering contract assertions or removing them from C++26;

In other words, they are playing a game of Chicken: “We believe you are going to give up first.”

They know full well that a failed C++26 will hurt everyone. But, because the WG21 process is so insane that a loss here risks killing Contracts entirely, and would require another three years of endless litigation and fights, the stakes are high.

As far as I know, the next scheduled WG21 meeting runs Nov 16â21, 2026 in BÃºzios. So, you might think “Ah, then it’s just a few days and they’ll sit down and sort things out, right?”

Well, probably not. The WG21 + ISO process is slow and messy. Even if everyone agrees on whether Contracts should/should not go in, each ballot is open for multiple weeks. So yeah, this may take another year or so.

If C++26 fails, I’ll pour one out. Not for you, but for the many, many people who tried to make you better, and failed3.

If you've made it this far, consider signing up for e-mail notifications, following along on Substack, or adding this blog to your RSS reader.

It’d be slightly easier to take Vinnie’s paper seriously if it didn’t contain Claude-isms like “The ‘purely additive’ claim turns the deferral into a dismissal” that make my eyes glaze over. There has been an uptick in AI usage within WG21, and not all of it has been responsible. ↩︎

Okay fine, there were some tiny concessions, P3878R1 decoupled parts of standard-library hardening from Contract observe mechanics. Still coupled to Contracts though, making it impossible to allow standard-library hardening to enter without Contracts getting in. In other words, the ‘standard-library hardening’ draft was written with the assumption that Contracts would definitely go in. ↩︎

This, for the record, will include the Contracts people (assuming Contracts fail). I am not a big fan of Contracts (for reasons unrelated to any of the discussion here), but I understand the case for them, and the people working on them are (like everyone else) victims of the process. ↩︎

#9874. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Uncorking Queueing Bottlenecks with OpenTelemetry

Oli Lane and Julian Wreford share how Gearset replaced guesswork in distributed asynchronous queues with OpenTelemetry tracing. They explain why traditional metrics fall short, how to implement user-centric SLOs based on latency distributions, and share practical debugging tips to help senior developers, software architects, and engineering leaders improve system reliability and team culture.

Julian Wreford is an engineering team lead at Gearset where he leads the team responsible for all things site reliability. Oli Lane is an Engineering Team Lead at Gearset. Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community.
