#9839. What are some "No AI" apps/companies/resources you know of?

Hey everyone I'm wondering if there's any useful/helpful list of apps, companies, or resources in general that avoid AI (they don't have to be vocally or openly "anti", but at least explicitly avoid it) that you know of?

I'm not looking to start a discussion on what's good/bad or (un)worthy about AI, or who's for/against, just links and/or communities promoting this sentiment/position.

For example, https://www.rebeltechalliance.org would be one of those resources.

https://codeberg.org/ethical-foss/ai-free-foss-alternatives

It's such a shame that a list titled "AI-free FOSS Alternatives" ends up becoming the opposite of its stated goal, with the top level section being "Tainted Software" and occasional sporadic little notes listing alternatives.

I like the steadfast anti-AI people even though I'm not really one of them, and I want them to thrive and carve out a lasting space online. Putting more focus on the positives of the anti-AI vision and way less on the rejection and refusal stuff would probably help with that, and I think this is a really clear example where the negative side of the message has stolen the show unnecessarily. The "tainted" list is inside baseball stuff and belongs in the equivalent of a Wikipedia talk page on there.

I strongly agree that it is better to fight for something good rather than against something bad. However, I find the list a very useful starting point. Studying it led me to the (startling to me) conclusion that the GNU/FSF vision is a positive one that encompasses the rejection of AI. There are probably others as well, but starting with GNU is not starting from scratch at least. Flipping positions on GNU was not on my personal philosophy bingo card for this year.

Putting more focus on the positives of the anti-AI vision and way less on the rejection and refusal stuff would probably help with that,

As a general rule, I think that "focus on the positives" is a good rule of thumb.

As a blanket rule, it doesn't work. Sometimes it's really about the negatives. If you're trying to convince people, say, not to smoke or do heroin... really, "it's great not being addicted to things" is not as strong a message as "you'll get lung cancer if you smoke" or "this is what heroin addiction does to people". (Granted "just say no" was also terrible as a campaign, but for different reasons.)

I'm not saying that AI usage is equivalent to heroin usage, exactly, but I'm not sure that "the positives of the anti-AI vision" is as persuasive as the arguments against generative AI.

where the negative side of the message has stolen the show unnecessarily

Again, I don't really agree with this. There are some things that it makes sense to be against. This is especially true in the case of generative AI in my opinion because of the way it spreads and has basically overrun the industry in a couple of years. For some of us, it's the black mold or asbestos of software. "Gee, having a house without black mold is so awesome" isn't really quite the same as "here's what black mold is going to do to you if it infests your house".

This list used to be called Open Slopware. I wrote about my personal relationship to it here: https://lobste.rs/s/unpaan/arborium_is_ai_slopware_should_not_be#c_twqzh3.

Mmmm not terribly surprising unfortunately.

Wrote down a few of my thoughts about it the other day actually.

Being overtly nasty might make you feel alive for a moment but it’s in conflict with any meaningful real-world goals, and it’s so normalised in anti-AI spaces that I’ve come to the conclusion that the whole thing is more about venting collective grief about unwanted change than achieving anything concrete.

Thanks, I wasn't aware of this list, though it shows very few alternatives (and I'm not saying they exist, but it almost makes it seem more helpless).

It also links to other resources but I think https://noai.starlightnet.work/list.html could be mainly what you're looking for.

I have been studying this list for the last few months. One of the main results is that I have gone back to Emacs. This is not my first go-round with it but I have found that nowadays it's much easier to get to a working IDE-like state than ever before. There are alternatives to most of the things I used to use within Emacs itself. I found that once I got over my initial reticence, it provides the kind of human-focused, malleable environment that I didn't realize I was missing.

One of the main results is that I have gone back to Emacs.

I am having trouble understanding the article you linked, but I note that it links to a potential fork of Emacs that would satisfy my requirements, so I think you actually have good news for me.

Well, I work there, but we are both a FOSS nonprofit and also have a firm no-gen-AI policy at the Spritely Institute, and do pretty cool decentralized network tech also

Recently made https://braincoded.software for this - it is not "anti", just "no".

Not much there for now apart from IRC channel, but I'm working on tiny invite-only link aggregator + public git and cvs repositories for members.

I understand offering alternatives to Git. I think mercurial deserves a lot more love than it gets.

But why Cvs specifically, over any number of other non-Git alternatives?

I honestly always liked Mercurial better over git, but sort of gave up at some point and moved all my stuff to git, feels weird to use both now especially since hg doesn't give me any portability perks over git.

Another one: https://codeberg.org/brib/slopfree-software-index

The "No AI" Webring is related - https://baccyflap.com/noai/

Similar to the rebel tech alliance, there's the trustworthy technology group. They have a Zulip chat you could join to discuss this further.

This is an academic's collection of materials: https://olivia.science/ai/

I'm putting together a software collective which is "anti-ai" as one of its core principles: https://conflagrate.software/

My idea is for it to be a safe, pleasant space for people to create and collaborate.

You are aware that the resource you link was made with a site builder that mentions an AI in the second sentence of their product hero? The resource was handmade, but not far away from AI.

Nice catch, but they used it before it was "AI-powered", which speaks a bit to the difficulty I'm facing trying to find alternatives to that.

Yes, sloppification is everywhere. Things that were once normal products now have an AI...

Rather than avoiding AI, why not opt for responsible usage of AI? LLMs speed things up, but it comes at a cost of losing correctness, which I do not think one can easily guarantee because of the way LLMs operate - statistically matching rather than logic/intuitive proofs which is what humans are good at. To get the best of both worlds, you want to use AI for smaller, more easily reviewed tasks, then use those (also w/ or w/out AI) to build a more complicated product.

I've no problem with not having to write out a bunch of code that can be written nearly identically by an AI. The QA and validation process is still a human endeavor and where you probably spend most of your time as a dev anyway. Actual coding amounts to no more than 20% of the time.

Nixing a tool like LLM is IMHO a bad idea, if it can help us save time and increase quality of output, then so be it.

I just don't want to use it. It doesn't interest me. I don't want to use things that used it either. I don't care if it "works better" or is "more efficient". It's okay to be a luddite.

I'm not looking to start a discussion on what's good/bad or (un)worthy about AI, or who's for/against, just links and/or communities promoting this sentiment/position.

Comments on posts about/for people who don't like and don't want to use AI which amount to "have you considered that AI isn't all bad actually?" are counterproductive and frankly really exhausting.

#9838. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Makes Agentic Workflows Generally Available with Isolation and Budget Controls

Nov 11, 2026 2 min read

GitHub has made GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available. The open-source project runs coding agents inside GitHub Actions for repository tasks such as issue triage and continuous integration (CI) failure analysis. Agents start with read-only permissions, and any changes they propose are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens.

That separation has limits. The project's FAQ says the protections do not automatically extend to direct write permissions or to custom jobs a workflow author adds, so the safety of a workflow depends on how it is configured. Authors can also add a GitHub Environment protection rule to require a reviewer before a write job runs.

Developers describe the work in natural-language Markdown, with YAML frontmatter for configuration. The project compiles that definition into a standard Actions workflow, which reuses existing runner groups and policy constraints, and teams can use Copilot or bring another coding agent. According to the general availability announcement, agents run in a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall, and a threat-detection job scans proposed changes before they are applied. The project entered public preview in June 2026.

Since the preview, GitHub has added support for Actions Runner Controller (ARC), its Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners, with Docker-in-Docker (DinD). DinD runs a Docker daemon inside the runner pod so the agent can start its sandbox containers. The project's guide notes that ARC runs the DinD sidecar as a privileged container by default, a privileged component sitting alongside an agent designed around least privilege.

Spending is capped by default. GitHub's documentation prices AI Credits (AIC) at $0.01 each and sets a cap of 1,000 AIC ($10) per run. The project's enterprise controls reference adds defaults of 5,000 AIC a day, 400 AIC per threat-detection run and a 20-minute timeout on the agent step, all of which organisations can override. The gh aw forecast command, no longer experimental, estimates monthly AI credit spending, including threat detection.

In the announcement, Ben Alton, senior manager in Accenture's Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team, said: "One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone." The announcement does not explain how that figure was measured.

Engineers testing the project have taken a more cautious line. In a walkthrough of an issue-triage workflow, Sascha Mirow-Stanitzok, team lead for middleware at freenet, judged the default budget far too generous for triage and capped his runs at 100 AIC, 15 turns and 10 minutes. He also wrote that telling the agent to ignore instructions in issue text does not protect a workflow by itself, and said he would not use the same pattern for workflows that change code or open pull requests.

GitLab takes a different route with its Duo Agent Platform flows, which run on runners under a composite identity that pairs a service account performing the actions with the human user who started the request. Its triggers, such as a mention or an assignment, must come from a human user, so one flow cannot start another. That rule stops agents from chaining work across flows without a person starting it.

GitHub's FAQ says conventional Actions remain the right choice for reproducible builds and tests, with agent workflows suited to tasks that need interpretation or generation. The project is available on GitHub Free, Team and Enterprise on github.com, and the default Copilot CLI engine requires a Copilot licence.

#9836. How do you actually self-host securely?

I recognize that the title is rather vague, but I'm completely green when it comes to self-hosting, so I figured here would be a good place to ask for some pointers given the discussions I sometimes see happening in the comments. I tried researching first through DDG and Google, but (and I recognize this might be a skill issue) most things I found are either SEO slop or trying to sell/market some service.

For some more context and to give a concrete example as to what I'm interested in, I got my hands on a Raspberry Pi which I'd like to use to start tinkering with self-hosting. My main goal would be to host my (static) website on it, potentially adding more things in the future.

Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting, so I'm curious whether it's viable to do it using open source tooling, any gotchas one might encounter, and generally any thoughts you might have on the topic.

(Also, feel free to suggest a tag other than devops, I figured security doesn't quite apply since it's a question and not a write-up/resource regarding security.)

It sounds like what you may want is "nobody can read my packets but me!" If that's the case I would look at the chain of things.

These three are super intertwined, "self hosting" is choosing which of these you want to own.

You may end up using nginx or haproxy somewhere to get ports to line up. But you can also use iptables. Dealer's choice.

Tailscale and Cloudflare tunnels are really cool. They take a bit of the headache away, but you're right that they give up that bit of security (and the learning!).

I'm so psyched for you :) let me know how it goes!

I just drove across the Untied States with my backup MX. My phone provided a hotspot, a GL.inet did tethering and provided Internet, and my backup MX ran a tinc tunnel to give itself a public IP.

Since my backup MX runs off of 5 volts (USB powered) and has a battery backup, I ran it off of the cigarette lighter USB power adapter, but it could've just as easily been off my solar panel (which I run through the hatchback window :)

I always picture it baking in the sun on the cracked back dash of a 1996 Toyota Camry flying down the highway.

I have to admit that I smiled at this too.

I'm not sure if acme.sh is the best choice.

Also, for a lot of self-hosting setups (where you've got a server at home with services that you want to reach from other devices), I'd argue that Tailscale is overkill. Plain Wireguard is pleasantly simple to configure.

Sure, it has some niceties - it has NAT traversal, it's smart enough to figure out more efficient routing than the star topology you'd probably end up with in the simplest plain wg setup, it has fancy multiple user support - but do you actually need any of that?

The reason (the only reason!) I'm using Tailscale instead of WireGuard is that Tailscale has native apps all over the place (including critically for Apple TV and Google's streamer-du-jour), whereas WireGuard doesn't.[1]. Given I don't have to pay anything to use Tailscale, that makes it worth it for me for at least that specific use-case.

[1]: Well, there's a paid subscription app for the Apple TV, and I could jailbreak the Google thing, but there's a limit to how much effort I wanna put into just getting my Jellyfin files available.

WireGuard is available on tvOS. Plain, free, open source WireGuard.

Oh awesome! I'll have to take another look. That was extremely not true in 2024 or '25

Uhhh I was so certain and yet… I think I hallucinated this. Doesn’t seem available.

I'd argue that Tailscale is overkill. Plain Wireguard is pleasantly simple to configure.

I keep hearing this, but I haven't seen anyone explain how to make this work nicely, and all of my forays into wg have been exercises in frustration (not that Tailscale has been pain-free). Getting the tunnel up and running works fine, but figuring out how to keep the tunnel from falling over or silently not forwarding traffic has been considerably more difficult.

Also, I'm not really sure how I would get wireguard working on my Apple TV without Tailscale.

use your pi to ssh to the box you rent, port forward 443 to your pi

When I tried this, the SSH tunnel would fall over all the time and need to be recreated. Seems like at a minimum you need some control loop to watch it, but even then sometimes the failure wasn't "the SSH process went away" but rather that it was alive but silently not working, and I couldn't figure out how to detect this case from the control loop running in the pi so I would have to kick it manually once or twice a month.

In my experience you can get decent reliability with autossh by setting the ServerAliveInterval so that there's always a trickle of traffic. You can also set TCPKeepAlive but since that operates at the TCP level it's subject to middleboxes, which I'd guess is a particular risk on a mobile network.

But I do agree that SSH is not the right tool here.

As a chronic putting stuff publicly accessible online guy, I'd say you get 95% of the way there by:

It's safer to start with services that aren't public facing, e.g. install Tailscale on your phone, laptop, and Raspberry Pi, and then start setting up services you want for yourself.

Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting

I like to do the end-to-end myself but sometimes I just can't be bothered and so use Cloudflare Tunnels to make it work, and that's a better outcome for me than giving up entirely.

I've heard about Tailscale many times but, to be honest, their website reads the same as corporate emails to me, as in I cannot digest any substance from it (might be another skill issue, I know). Would you mind sharing some concrete use case for it (e.g. an example of what you use it for)? That might make it easier for me to grasp the concept.

The simplest way to explain it I think would be to say that Tailscale makes all your devices act like they’re on the same home network, no matter where they actually are.

Their site from 2020 is a bit clearer: https://web.archive.org/web/20201129111934/https://tailscale.com/

But basically it lets your various devices connect to each other, whereever they are, without having to deal with port forwarding, firewalls, dynamic DNS... so your phone or laptop can access self-hosted services on your Raspberry Pi (photos, Jellyfin, RSS, files, ...). It does this while keeping it all hidden from random people/attackers.

I don't use Tailscale, and instead just use plain Wireguard/mTLS, but Tailscale is easiest to set up and seems to be the most popular option for people that want to access their Raspberry Pi when away from home.

I primarily use it for a personal "private intranet"; I host services like Grafana and Forgejo on homelab machines inside my home, and then connect them to Tailscale so I can access them remotely through the tailnet without needing to put them on the public internet. As a bonus it also provides "funnel", a public reverse-proxy which works the same as serving to the tailnet, avoiding the need for a public IP to serve those services.

Unlike traditional VPNs, Tailscale does not tunnel traffic through its infrastructure per se - the control plane server governs access and routing, but traffic transits through establishing point-to-point WireGuard tunnels, with Tailscale operating relays which forward encrypted packets between machines when needed for e.g. NAT traversal. That said, you do give up some amount of self hosting - you can rent a cheap VPS and set up e.g. Headscale to get a decent subset of functionality (though I personally haven't tried this myself).

Tailscale is decent, but if you want to do some learning, I recommend setting up a WireGuard tunnel manually.

My setup is a cloud VPS (on OVH) running TLS termination, which forwards traffic to my homelab server, which connects up to the VPS over WireGuard. That way, my home IP is not publicly visible, and it doesn't matter if it changes or whatever -- my homelab server just reconnects the tunnel and the cloud VPS addresses it by its WireGuard IP.

Specific example: say you want to have a job server whose dashboard you can access via a stable identifier, runs on an isolated machine, and is not exposed to the public internet. Then Tailscale is a great solution. Other examples: tunnels into other VPCs which should not be exposed to the internet; sharing local demos between those in the network; using a specific machine as an exit node when you don’t trust the network you’re currently on; access your devices via stable IDs (eg I have a cluster of Macs whose IPs are dynamic, but I can log in via screen share with stable IDs)

It's simply a way to set up a VPN to your home network. The thing that makes it attractive is that you don't need a static IP for your home to connect to as they do routing through them and it is extremely easy to set up.

But it also means you are trusting them. Personally I do have a static IP at home and my router also supports WireGuard so I am using that. Same thing.

The best high-level overview of why Tailscale came to be, IMO, is https://tailscale.com/blog/two-internets-both-flakey

Ten mentions of Tailscale in this conversation already, I'm going to make it 11.

It really does solve the home lab security problem so well.

Run it on your devices - it works in everything (I even have it on an Apple TV) and it's trivial to install and configure.

Now your phone or laptop, anywhere in the world, can securely talk to the other devices via their 100. IPs (or through Tailscale DNS) - and nothing else can reach them.

And it's free for that kind of personal use!

Prior to Tailscale I was too afraid to even try running a home lab of any sort. Now I have several devices on mine and I actually use them remotely (from my phone) several times a week.

Sometimes I deliberately leave my laptop at home because controlling it from my phone while I'm out and about is more efficient than physically getting it out of my bag.

(Tailscale is basically just a wrapper around Wireguard, so if you want to roll your own you can - I'm not nearly confident enough in my own skills to attempt that for something as security-critical as this myself.)

As an alternative to Tailscale I do the same with ZeroTier, which I think predates it (I actually started doing it with an in-house technology we had at a defunct startup called Lima...)

Here're some broad generalzations that may help you.

First, yes, most of what you find using search engines is poor quality, regurgitated marketing stuff. Sure, you can learn good things from those results, but you'll also learn poor practices at the same time. For instance, most marketed how-tos will tell you to download binary programs or Docker images, which might be OK for learning, but become security issues over time.

One good practice is to learn how to install software via source, or at least using a package manager that's updated often. Docker images are made when the creators feel like it, and often have dependencies baked in that are ancient and may have vulnerabilities. A proper packaging system that's updated often will use the same dependencies for all of your software and will be updated regularly, particularly when any of those dependencies have exploitable vulnerabilities.

Learn about and become comfortable with the Unix permissions model. It's actually quite good, and what some of these marketing people will tell you is wrong: if you use a separate, unprivileged user for each service you host, and one of those users gets compromised, and it can lead to a root escalation, then the issue is that your system isn't updated enough to not allow a root escalation. The number of people who want you to address the symptom and not the problem is huge, and they often advocate for, for instance, Docker or some other thing because it's popular, not because it actually makes sense.

Don't let feature creep win. I host dozens of Wordpress sites for friends and small businesses, and every time PHP gets updated, someone's site ends up not working because they got excited when setting up their site and install a dozen plugins, most which aren't necessary, but which aren't updated and cause their site to stop working with the latest PHP. I've gotten good at disabling plugins without logging in to WP. It's better to only install and use what you really want to use.

Related to that, I recommend installing, playing, getting everything working properly, making notes, then using those notes to reinstall from scratch so you know which steps are superfluous. Your first install might have twenty steps, but once you understand things, the second might have six. Clean is good.

Avoid passwords everywhere you can. Use ssh keys, only allow access to https login pages to certain IPs or IP ranges, if possible, make those links custom if you can, and so on. An OpenCloud login page that people (and bots) don't know is worlds better than a public one that bots will hit constantly.

For anything that does require passwords, don't reuse, don't use simple or basic passwords, and don't let anyone get away with thinking their weak password is "good enough" or that nobody will find the service to try too hard to log in. Assume everything will get tested, including every username, email address and password in every leak, ever.

Don't believe gatekeepers that tell you that you can't, that you shouldn't do certain things. I've taught people who are non-technical to self-host email. If non-technical people can do it, then why should gatekeepers who claim to be technically proficient be believed when they insist that email can't reasonably be self-hosted?

If you find yourself in communities of people who are condescending to you, or who are trying to tell you that a Raspberry Pi isn't a proper server, for instance, then find another community. This community is a good one :)

Oh - get good, durable storage for your Pi, and have fun!

For only a static website? Only allow SSH private keys, no passwords. Run stable versions of stable distros and patch whenever something bad happens. Use nginx. Turn off everything you don't need, and use a firewall to double-check.

Using a VPN to a server elsewhere is useful, but mainly as a way to avoid having to talk a residential ISP into allowing you to serve websites and such. I like Nebula more than Tailscale, it's a bit chonky to set up but works magically well once it's up. Tried Wireguard and it seemed to have real issues with hole-punching.

A very non-concrete advice is simplicity.

When you self-host, you're responsible for security yourself (duh). And maintenance is gonna be a hobby. So scale accordingly: Choose software that doesn't aim to change from under your feet, because that'll make you put off maintenance (this is what some of us like to use the word "stable" to mean). Choose software that's easy to get back into and understand without having to be in the weeds every day. Choose software that'll at least break in obvious ways. Choose software where lots of things have to go wrong for things to break.

How much you need to care about security is entirely dependent on what you host. I would for example greatly invested in security if I self-hosted a public facing file storage or an email server.

I would in general care much less if as you describe I would be hosting a static website on a Raspberry Pi. The risk just isn't that big. It can't cost you a lot of money since it's your own hardware. The worst thing that could happen is that a stranger gains complete control over your Raspberry Pi. They could possibly probe your local network (but not if you put the Rasberry Pi on a subnet), display other information on your website or put your Rasberry Pi to work on something benefitting them (as part of a botnet or crypto mining for example).

I personally wouldn't consider any of those possibilities as great risks. And as a bonus, setting up logging to detect if any of these were happening could be a fun side project.

I avoid exposing my services to the public internet since I am the only user. They are available only via WireGuard. I use plan WireGuard, but solutions like Tailscale or NetBird are fine if you need something else to deal with configuration for you.

On top of that, I still do HTTPs everywhere (using the ACME DNS-01 challenge so I get proper certificates from Let's Encrypt without exposing anything on the public Internet).

Authentication is mostly based on passkeys (I use PocketID for single-sing-on) and I only use SSH keys (backed by secure enclaves whenever possible).

I run my services in NixOS. For my threat model it's okay to run everything on the same machine but to get more workload segregation you could separate the various services across several VMs/micro-VMs.

I described my NAS setup here: https://arne.me/blog/buildlog-nas#security, tl;dr is Tailscale with self-hosted control server, nothing exposed to the internet, HTTPS, encrypted drives.

I think self-hosting a website from your home and self-hosting other things like storage/rss/photos/etc. should be treated as distinct problems with different approaches. Ideally they shouldn't live on the same system even.

Several years ago, I wrote down how I do it, step-by-step. I still use mostly the same approach, though some of the steps have changed over the years. The biggest difference is that now I use tailscale for new things, and and have my reverse proxy connect to the backend over the tailnet. Tailscale is essentially automating the wireguard setup I described in that post, while adding a few nice features around it.

I like having my own reverse proxy VPS. The cheapest possible Linux VPS from whatever provider you want works fine for this. For new VPSes, netcup is my current favorite. (I also use Hetzner, DigitalOcean and Linode for some projects. They are a little easier to navigate than netcup, and all 3 are available for smaller units of time than a month. For things that will be online for a full month or more, though, netcup's pricing is hard to beat. It does make me chuckle that I'm paying in euros for a server I could bike past on the east coast of the US.)

But if you're only hosting things for yourself and for people you trust on your network, you could skip the reverse proxy VPS and just use your wireguard network/tailnet.

Most things I self host are private use anyway. So my home server only gets network access and I use WireGuard to access things remotely.

This of course doesn't apply to a public facing static website. I'd honestly never host those from home network since that also provides people visiting it with too much geo information than I'd like. So for that I'd rent a VPS and keep it as simple as possible. Either nginx with the lets encrypt certbot or caddy which has certificates build in and also supports static websites.

Make sure security updates are automatically applied, make ssh key only and you already have most of your bases covered as far as static hosting goes.

instead of a cloudflare tunnel you could grab a vps, and set up a wireguard tunnel with NAT. I do this for my torrent and DirectConnect clients, so they get public IPs without UPnP/NAT-PMP. I am considering doing same for Jellyfin so it's available outside of tailscale. But I might still require some extra layer, not sure.

I'm lazy and not a good model, so maybe dont do what I do but:

I have WireGuard set up on my OPNsense box so I can VPN into my home network when I'm out. Services I want on the public internet are just open on 443, mostly static sites but a couple of things like Jellyfin. Services I don't want public have a default deny all in my Nginx config with a whitelist for my LAN and Wireguard subnets. I containerize stuff, idk, I figure if some container escape gets discovered then I'm not the biggest target anyway hopefully I have (encrypted) backups at rsync.net in case anything goes down

That's basically the gist. I guess I also keep my nftables fairly locked down on my server and have Crowdsec to block known bad IPs and can detect some things like port scans and block those too + IP-location based blocking on OPNsense to fully block connections from, e.g. China and Russia,

As you can't control upcoming exploits, you want to:

Reducing the access: Some only allow access to these ports: 22 for SSH (if you leave it on standard port, which you will see some people advise to change), 80 (normally never used except to ease SSL setup via Let's encrypt), and 443 (only for services that need to be public). For the services not intended to general public, people would use a VPN or Tailscale, which means only people you allow on the network will be able to access these (it means you will likely need to help your family member and friends to setup Twingate if you want them to access these, and they won't be able to reach your services from any laptop). Some people find the above even too open, and would reduce it further. Everything is behind tailscale (even SSH), and public services leverage Tailscale Funnel. No port is open on your machine, but a tunnel exist between your machine and tailscale infrastructure that expose your websites there. Reducing impact: The public websites can still be vulnerable to zero days (from tailscale funnel or not), so the idea is containing damage. Run your services in a containers is an easy way to limit impact to that service only if things go wrong (and not the whole server).

If you want to go a bit more advanced, I found this blog contains good advice generally:

There are obviously much more you can do: VLAN for your home server, and a lot of permutation for the same idea: wireguard instead of tailscale, iroh instead of tailscale, VM instead of containers, different service users instead of containers, etc.

I run two reverse proxies: one is publicly accessible, and one is only accessible over WireGuard. The public reverse proxy can only communicate with the public services (e.g. website), and the private one can only communicate with the private services (e.g. Immich). The services can only talk to the reverse proxy and aren't exposed in any other way. This is all done using basic Docker networking.

There are a lot of posts about Tailscale already, but I prefer WireGuard. It's trivial to set up, and there's no magic involved. Some serious missteps by Tailscale, such as this incident, and general enshittification concerns make me not want to use it.

I wrote a simple script to manage and distribute my WireGuard configs and deal with the various edge cases my setup has, but you can also just copy your configs to your devices manually. It really isn't as big of a deal as some people make it out to be.

grsecurity + PaX + RBAC rules, possibly using learn feature to build up ruleset

When configuring the grsec kernel, ensure to set up the socket limitation groups, GIDs which cannot open sockets (or flip it to require membership to open sockets "nosocks vs allowsocks")

Audit the system for setuid executables and, creating similar groups, limit access to them to certain users. If users cannot access a vulnerable SUID executable, they cannot exploit it.

Ensure to set sane limits.conf to avoid forkbombs.

Ring fence stuff with UIDs - one user, one service. That way a hacked service can leak its own stuff and not much more.

Don't rely on containers, sandboxes, or magic solutions. Real security is boring. Boring usually works. Docker, firejail, Podman, cgroups, etc all add code on top of the already-running access control and permissions, and in modern times, more code means more bugs.

Things like SEL4 would be perfectly secure on verified hardware, but that says nothing of the applications you build on top of them.

I, uh, am surprised there are people running grsec for self-hosted stuff. I wouldn't have budget to get that.

Lots of great advice here for a "standard" Web server setup. I wanted to mention that there are some less standard approaches, like P2P and overlay networks, which can side-step issues like tunnelling, DNS and HTTPS.

For example, TOR has a feature called "onion services", where any Internet-connected machine can make a port accessible via a .onion address (I used this twenty years ago to run a Wiki from my dorm room; despite knowing very little about networking!)

Static Website hosting is also a pretty good fit for content-addressed storage like IPFS, dat, freenet, etc.

The downside to these approaches is that they're not quite compatible with a standard OS + DNS + Web browser setup. In the best case, that can be avoided via a gateway like Tor2web or an IPFS gateway; but in the worst case it might require installing a particular client in order to access. That might be fine for applications where you just want to connect together machines that you control.

I assume your internet connection has enough bandwidth to sustain a small to moderate website. Self-hosting a publicly facing service is an order of magnitude more dangerous than self-hosting private services such as photo management applications or media servers because of the security implications. On the bright side, static pages can be hosted securely with relatively low effort compared to LAMP stack.

(a) Applying network segmentation is a good start. The RPi should not be able to communicate with other devices through router / firewall configuration. Maybe allow just one device based on IP or MAC address to access the RPi from the LAN.

(b) Then setup DNS records. I assume you own an FQDN. Use an ready-made or custom script to update the DNS records. I'm using dnscontrol alongside envsubst and to perform the changes but there are simpler solutions out there.

(c) Once the DNS is working and updating properly, use an application to issue SSL certificates. My favourite is acme.sh but there are quite a few polished alternatives, e.g. certbot, lego, etc.

(d) Now you're ready to setup a reverse proxy. Note that modern rev-proxies like Caddy can manage (c) on their own. I'm not using them, I'm familiar with nginx so I use that.

(e) Create a deployment user with minimum permissions and use that user to upload data via sftp or other secure protocol. If you want to setup a deployment pipeline via git, that's also possible through webhooks.

(f) Secure the system. I'm pretty sure that you can flat-out ban the big cloud CIDRs. That will save you from dumb scanners abusing your website. Since very few humans use these addresses for outgoing connections, I think it's a good strategy to block them straight-up. You can setup a cron script to download CIDRs and update your firewall "block" tables.

f.1 Make sure you setup some sort of monitoring, so that you can quickly measure things like resources and even incoming requests (e.g. response latency, No of incoming requests, etc). Since you're going to self-host you'll have log access which means full visitors info.

f.2 You might want to explore the possibility of setting a "chroot"

f.3 Alerting: pushover is a good "host -> mobile" alternative, another is to setup the SMTPd in a way that the system can send you emails with status reports, etc. to your personal email.

(g) Backup everything locally (e.g. another NAS) or remotely (backblaze is fairly cheap), or both.

Many people suggest some publicly facing tunnel / proxy server, but doesn't this defeat the purpose of self-hosting: if you are running a VPS proxy, why not just host things on that proxy? If you're using some VPN service, why not just use AWS or something? Self-hosting loses its independence.

Well, conceptually yes, in practice it's a trade-off between security & convenience. If you tunnel to a cloud service the traffic, you still own the data and most of the infra, and just delegating data passing to an external service (I wouldn't rent a whole VPS for that though, and just leverage off-the-shelf solutions like Tailscale or Cloudfare) You can still do the same without these external services (Headscale or Wireguard self hosted, and/or a proxy for the few public facing websites), it's all a trade-off about what you want to manage.

A VPS proxy can be just a gateway into your network, and you don't need much resources for WireGuard. A tiny VPS at $5-12 per year is enough. Your machines at home likely have more resources to host the applications.

To echo the other comments in this thread so far, I've similarly used the Tailscale/Cloudflare Tunnel combination. Tailscale for "personal" services (Syncthing, remote wake-up, etc.) while the Cloudflare tunnel is for anything publicly available (e.g a library site). Yes, definitely less learning than trying to full roll up your own infrastructure, but it's free and fairly painless while giving me a bit more flexibility w.r.t how I'm hosting services.

Anders Pitman had collected a boatload of resources regarding this:

https://github.com/anderspitman/awesome-tunneling

Both closed and open source solutions are listed.

From looking at it just now, it still seems to be actively maintained

Services like cloudflare tunnels have little to do with security. The problem they solve is getting incoming internet traffic to a server without a public IP address. Those are very different problems.

Some ISPs give out fixed public facing IPv4 address. If this is the case, set up port forwarding and enjoy. Otherwise, you'll need a reverse proxy service. Cloudflare tunnels is an option, but it's also easy to run your own on a rented server. (which can also work for non-HTTP services)

In any case, proxy based systems will introduce a dependency on some other server. If you don't like this, go complain to your ISP.

If your router at home is capable to forward a port, do a http port forwarding to your raspberry pi, get your public ip and put it in your dns. Note sure what you mean with security but an exploit on http is pretty small for a static website. If you want more security put your site in docker with a user other than root. Lot of fun, a lot to learn.

One thing I don't see mentioned here is---if you host a web site, your ISP connection will be swamped with bot activity if it's publicly available. There are multiple ways to mitigate this, but they all come with different tradeoffs; Cloudflare is easy to set up, but you are relying upon a huge corporation that is part of the web consolidation problem. The other solution is to tune your web server/firewall to limit concurrent connections/block traffic, but that's more work on your side.

Personally, I do self-host, but it's a VM server that I manage myself. It's not a ton of work, but I do keep an eye on it and have had to spend quite a bit more time than I wanted in tuning Apache (which I've been using for 25+ years) not to fall over (to the point of compiling it myself with a custom module to limit IP connections).

You can start small and (relatively) safe and use CloudFlare to give you free DNS, TLS certs, a Tunnel that'll let you sidestep a lack of static IP (if you don't have such a thing) and put you behind their infrastructure.

You can then take steps towards running your own pieces of that, as you gain confidence.

Making your own TLS certs is pretty easy, using Let's Encrypt, and there's plenty of tooling to run that for you automatically if you just run through its setup process.

Running your own DNS can also be easy, and there's plenty of material to read. If it's a site that you don't mind dropping off the web occasionally if (when) you're waiting for DNS to propagate after you messed up an entry, just do it and enjoy!

Not really an answer to your question, but I think hosting publicly accessible sites for broader access through your home internet is a bad idea, because if you get real traffic going to it, you are likely in violation of your ISP's policies and risk ending up in a bad position in the future. Home internet is how I work, so if I lost it, I would be hurting. You're also opening yourself up to getting your home internet DDOS'd, which would also hurt quite a bit and make your ISP grumpy.

If your site is static, you can host a static site completely for free with Cloudflare R2, and publish it easily via wrangler. No need to expose your home network in any way for a static site, that seems like overkill to me. I understand it's about learning and tinkering and so on, but the amount of learning and tinkering you're going to do while hosting a static site is basically nil. Personally I think there is more learning to be done figuring out how to generate a static site and publish it automatically via wrangler. This is also a great way to run a Wordpress site as you can use Wordpress safely on your home network, use a static site plugin to generate the site, publish it with wrangler, and avoid all the 'hacking' attempts that come from having a Wordpress site.

Personally, I run all of my homelab services inside containers and expose them via Cloudflared, and I know you already dismissed this, but I am not quite sure why as the only thing Cloudflared does is terminate TLS and eliminate issues with residential dynamic IPs. Other solutions for handling this are just as automated these days (caddy, nginx+certbot, etc), there's little difference and not much learning to do there.

I think ~mw and ~marginalia have covered most of the advice I would give. The only thing I have to add to that is that for hosting larger amounts of services, NixOS is the only operating system I will use. Its packages (nixpkgs) have good defaults -- most services have extensive sandboxing already set up for you -- and it provides for one place where all the vulnerability-knobs (i.e. open ports, weird user permissions, etc) can be found. It also forces you to be very explicit about security. If there are any services / dependencies with critical CVEs, it will refuse to build until you enter their names and versions verbatium into the configuration file. This is simultaneously good motivation to not run vulnerable software, and also serves to alert you if you missed a vulnerability report.

Though for hosting smaller amounts of software, really whatever's fine. I run Alpine Linux with HAProxy on my VPS. Just make sure you understand the system, and update it frequently.

In theory I agree with what most people wrote, but I kinda exactly don't want to expose any machine on the LAN to the internet, not even just by port forwarding https.

Maybe one day I'll make a local VM that has no connectivity to the lan so a potential attacker would need to break out of that VM first.

Plus the problems with DNS and addressing hosts from the LAN and from outside, but maybe I have not read the tailscale docs 100% correctly.

Used to have my apps exposed to the internet for ease of access but following the stream of AI hacks, got Tailscale and it turned out really way to setup and use. There’s also an open source version called Headscale that you can self host. My apps reside on a Pi I have under my desk and also a free Oracle VM.

#9834. Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Keep the three repositories side by side:

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:

After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:

The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md, then serve it with vLLM.

From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.
