Up/down rotational motion around the horizontal axis.

Table 24: Secondary camera-motion activity durations in SDG-SynHuman. Secondary motions are compositional layers that may overlap temporally, therefore reported durations are independent per-motion totals rather than shares of a fixed duration budget.

The dataset is delivered in 1,215 tar shards under shards/, each bundling 200 samples. Per sample (keyed by UUID): RGB as H.264 in video/uuid.mp4; FFV1 lossless 1080p depth in depth/uuid.mkv with a companion JSON recording depth range, resolution, frame rate, and dtype for metric reconstruction; per-frame camera data in meta/uuid_camera.json; scene-level metadata in metas/uuid.json (environment, lighting, agents, camera configuration, animation tasks); and asset-level metadata in description/uuid.json (spawned inventory, motion assets, placements, provenance). All annotations are generated deterministically from the USD scene graph. Fig. 34 shows sample RGB and depth outputs, for both the exterior and interior views.

SDG-Warehouse (PhysicsAI-WorldModel-Synthetic-Warehouse-Operation-Scenes) is a synthetic video dataset of indoor industrial-safety events rendered in fully simulated warehouse environments. Real surveillance footage of these events is rare, hard to release at scale, and seldom carries the kind of dense ground truth that physical-AI training benefits from, so we generate it in simulation, where the event is guaranteed to happen, every parameter is controllable, and every frame is paired with deterministic per-pixel and per-object annotations. The release covers four representative scenarios—a forklift–human near-miss (23%), a warehouse fire with worker evacuation (36%), a forklift–shelf collision (20%), and a warehouse box-pickup action (21%)—totaling ∼123K clips (∼412 hours of video) at 1920×1080 and 30 fps, with multiple synchronized camera viewpoints per simulation run.

All four scenarios are built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Procedural scene composition—warehouse layout, shelf placement, prop variation, and per-light randomization of color temperature, intensity, exposure, and color—is handled by Isaac Sim Replicator Object (IRO). Agent and sensor population—worker spawning and behavior, forklift placement and navigation, and the camera rigs that define the dataset’s multi-view viewpoints—is handled by Isaac Sim Replicator Agent (IRA). Camera placement is parametric, with height, distance, and look-down angle sampled per run, and worker assets and motions are sampled from Isaac Sim’s character library to diversify human appearance and gait. Each simulation run is seeded with a unique random seed that controls all randomized variables (scene composition, lighting, agent identity and motion, camera pose, and event timing), so runs are independent and reproducible.

Each camera viewpoint provides an H.264 RGB clip with synchronized per-frame annotations: metric depth (raw plus log-normalized colorized variant); instance segmentation (per-pixel IDs traceable to specific simulated objects, with a colorized variant); shaded segmentation (3D-aware rendering with normal-based shading); a Canny edge map computed on the shaded segmentation; 2D tight and loose axis-aligned bounding boxes plus 3D oriented bounding boxes for every tracked agent and prop; and per-frame camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Each annotation stream is also released as an encoded video alongside the RGB clip. Run-level structured metadata records scenario type, random seed, asset and agent inventory, event parameters (e.g., forklift dodge distance, fire ignition location, exit waypoints), and lighting randomization. Figure 35 shows the modalities for one frame per scenario.

Figure 35: SDG-Warehouse dataset. Sample view of the four scenarios and the annotations (RGB clips, metric depth, instance segmentation, shaded segmentation, and Canny edge).

Figure 36: Joint embedding geometry of pre-train and SDG. PCA→UMAP projection of 20,000 pre-training cluster centroids (gray) and 200 randomly sampled clips from each SDG source. Each SDG source forms a distinct, tightly clustered region that overlaps only narrowly with the bulk pre-training distribution.

To verify that synthetic content is genuinely complementary to the pre-training corpus, we analyze its position in the Cosmos-Embed1 video embedding space relative to clusters from the pre-training distribution. Fig. 36 visualizes the joint geometry of pre-training and SDG embeddings, while Tab. 25 quantifies the distance from each SDG source to the pre-training manifold using an in-distribution self-reference as a baseline. Together, these results show that SDG occupies long-tail regions of the embedding space that are not sufficiently covered by web-scale pre-training alone.

We study how different synthetic data generation (SDG) sources affect video generation quality and domain understanding by fine-tuning our pre-trained model (Cosmos3-Nano) on each source individually and jointly. We evaluate all variants using PAIBench-G T2V benchmark (Zhou et al., 2025c), which reports an overall score, a perceptual Quality score, and six domain-specific sub-scores: Common Sense, AV (autonomous vehicles), Robot, Industry, Human, and Physics. Results are summarized in Tab. 26.

Table 26: Ablation study on synthetic data generation (SDG) datasets, evaluated on PAIBench-G T2V (Zhou et al., 2025c). Each model is fine-tuned from the same pre-trained baseline with data from one SDG source; SDG-All mixes all five sources. Bold denotes improvement over the baseline; underline marks the best score in each column. Colored deltas show change relative to the baseline (green = improvement, red = degradation).

A consistent pattern across all SDG variants is that each source lifts different domain-specific scores, reflecting the unique content distribution of each simulator. SDG-DriveSim yields the largest gain in the Robot domain (+0.89) and a strong Common Sense improvement (+0.52), reflecting the rich structured dynamics of driving scenarios. SDG-RobotSim improves perceptual Quality most among all sources (+0.26) and moderately lifts the Robot score (+0.23). SDG-Warehouse provides broad positive deltas across Overall, Domain, AV (+0.29), and Physics (+0.21), while maintaining strong in Robot (+0.60). SDG-PhyxSim delivers the largest single-domain gain: a +0.85 uplift in Industry and a +0.80 gain in Robot, driven by its physics-grounded industrial and manipulation content. SDG-SynHuman is the standout individual source, posting the best overall score (79.79) with the highest positive deltas in Domain (+0.29), Common Sense (+0.66), AV (+0.47), and Robot (+1.23). The breadth of human-centric synthetic content appears to provide a strong general-purpose signal that transfers across multiple evaluation domains.

The most consistent pattern of degradation across all SDG sources is the Human domain score, which drops in every single variant without exception—ranging from −0.38 (SDG-SynHuman) to −0.69 (SDG-PhyxSim). Notably, even SDG-SynHuman, which is specifically built from synthetic human-centric scenes, fails to recover this score. This suggests that the sim-to-real gap is particularly pronounced for human-related visual content: current simulators do not yet replicate the subtle appearance, motion, and behavioral nuances of real humans with sufficient fidelity to benefit this evaluation domain. More broadly, domain-specialized sources can also degrade orthogonal categories—SDG-RobotSim hurts AV (−1.03) and Industry (−1.22), while SDG-PhyxSim’s physics emphasis comes with notable AV degradation (−1.42)—underscoring the need to mix sources rather than rely on any single simulator.

Mixing all SDG sources (SDG-All) yields uniformly positive deltas across eight of nine metrics, with only Human showing a residual dip (−0.47), consistent with the sim-to-real gap observed above. It achieves the best Quality score (72.56) and consistent improvements across all other domain categories, demonstrating that data diversity suppresses individual source biases. Based on these results, our final model incorporates the SDG datasets together with real, high-quality videos during a dedicated mid-training stage. This design allows the model to absorb the domain-specific physical understanding encoded in synthetic data while retaining the perceptual fidelity and visual realism it acquired from real footage in pre-training.

Cosmos3-Edge uses a dense 2B backbone trained from scratch. Its training follows a two-stage curriculum: pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning. The pre-training stage is further divided into base pre-training and long-context extension. We use BF16 precision throughout training; optimizer settings are given below.

During base pre-training, we train the 2B Edge backbone from scratch on a total of 15T tokens from the Nemotron pre-training corpus, using a sequence length of 8,192 tokens. This stage consists of two sub-stages: general pre-training on a broad-coverage data mixture, followed by continued pre-training on a higher-quality mixture. The data mixture is hot-swapped during training: continued pre-training resumes from the general-pre-training checkpoint while preserving the optimizer state and learning-rate schedule, so only the data mixture changes. We use AdamW with peak learning rate 1.2×10−3, (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at norm 1.0. We use a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule, aligning the data-mixture switch with the transition from the stable phase to the decay phase. The tokenizer is shared with the NVIDIA Nemotron-3 models (NVIDIA, 2025f).

During the long-context extension phase, we extend the context window of the Cosmos3-Edge backbone to 128K tokens. Although the extended context window supports 128K-token training sequences, the primary goal of this stage is to improve robustness and quality at the deployed 32K-token sequence length. During the context extension phase, we train on 128K sequence length with an increased RoPE base of 1e8. We use a constant learning rate of 1.2×10−5 and the long-context phase is trained with 90B tokens. For the data blend in this phase, we downsample the pre-training blend to 80% and add long document QA data as the remaining 20% in the blend.

We use the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data from Nemotron-Cascade-2 (Yang et al., 2026b), which covers a broad set of domains including mathematics, coding, science, general chat, instruction following, tool use, and code-agent tasks. In total, the dataset contains approximately 26M SFT samples. We pack these examples into sequences of up to 128K tokens, yielding roughly 2.6M packed training samples. The model is trained in a single SFT stage with a global batch size of 32. We use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 2×10−5 and (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.98). Empirically, model capability peaks after approximately 1.7 epochs, corresponding to 140K training steps.

We evaluate our SFT model on a set of text benchmarks spanning reasoning, science, instruction following, long context, and general capabilities: HMMT25 Feb (Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament, 2025), GPQA (Rein et al., 2023), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024d), AA-LCR (Artificial Analysis Team, 2025), IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025a), and Scale AI Multi-Challenge (Sirdeshmukh et al., 2025). We compare against Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026b), a strong baseline with the same model size.

As shown in Tab. 27, our text SFT model substantially outperforms Qwen3.5-2B on math reasoning and science benchmarks, such as HMMT25 Feb and GPQA. It yields comparable results on instruction-following and long-context evaluations, including IFBench and AA-LCR. However, it lags behind Qwen3.5-2B on general-domain benchmarks such as MMLU-Pro.

Table 27: Text benchmark results. Comparing Cosmos3-Edge and Qwen3.5-2B across reasoning, science, instruction-following, and long-context evaluations. Cosmos3-Edge substantially improves mathematical and scientific reasoning capability on HMMT25 Feb and GPQA, while achieving comparable scores on IFBench and AA-LCR.

While the main experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Cosmos 3 across a wide range of understanding and generation tasks, they do not fully isolate the contributions of individual design choices. To better understand the factors underlying the model’s capabilities, we conduct a series of ablation studies examining key architectural, data, and training decisions. These studies investigate how the Reasoner and Generator interact within the Mixture-of-Transformers framework, the impact of multimodal training signals such as audio and action data, the effectiveness of temporal conditioning mechanisms, and the transferability of learned world and action representations across domains. Together, these analyses provide deeper insight into the design principles that enable Cosmos 3 to function as a unified omnimodal world model for Physical AI.s

In this study, we investigate how the Reasoner benefits the Generator model. We train two models using the Cosmos3-Nano architecture: one with Qwen3-VL-8B as the understanding tower, and the other with our Cosmos3-Nano Reasoner. In both cases, the Generator tower is trained from scratch. For this ablation, we restrict training to 256p and 480p resolutions with clip lengths of 0–200 frames, and set the sequence length to 25K. Following our large-scale run, we use joint image–video training. Both models are trained for 90K iterations on 256 GPUs. We report PAIBench scores for both below.

Table 28: Understanding tower ablation. We report domain and quality scores on PAIBench T2V and I2V for two variants that differ only in the pretrained model used to initialize the understanding tower while the Generator tower is trained from scratch: (1) Cosmos 3 Reasoner and (2) Qwen3-VL. Subject and background consistency are I2V-specific and not applicable to T2V. Initializing the understanding tower from the Cosmos3 Reasoner yields better domain scores on Physical AI domains than the Qwen3-VL variant.

As shown in Table 28, replacing Qwen3-VL-8B with our Cosmos3-Nano Reasoner in the understanding tower yields consistent improvements in domain scores, particularly in Physical AI domains. On T2V, the Reasoner improves the overall Domain score from 73.7 to 75.7, with the largest gains concentrated in physically-grounded categories: Robot (+4.8, 66.5 → 71.3), Physics (+0.5, 88.7 → 89.2), AV (+2.3, 52.6 → 54.9), and Industry (+1.0, 77.4 → 78.4). A similar pattern holds on I2V, where the Domain score rises from 80.0 to 80.8, driven by gains in Common sense (+0.7), Industry (+0.8), Human (+1.0), and Physics (+0.2). These results suggest that the reasoner provides better embeddings for Physical AI domains for generator to learn. The quality scores for both models are comparable.

We study two complementary mechanisms for conditioning generation on a target frame rate: (i) MRoPE FPS modulation, which scales the temporal axis of the unified 3D MRoPE by the target FPS, and (ii) Text Control, which injects the target duration and FPS as natural-language text inside the structured JSON caption. For this ablation, we restrict training to 256p and 480p resolutions with clip lengths of 0–200 frames, and set the sequence length to 25K. Following our large-scale run, we use joint image–video training. We train 4 models for 130K iterations on 128 GPUs each, varying only whether each mechanism is active: Base (no control), Text Control (text only), MRoPE FPS Modulation (MRoPE only), and Text Control + MRoPE FPS Modulation (both). We curate an evaluation set with known source duration and FPS, ∼100 videos each of 10, 15, 24, 30 FPS (±2 FPS tolerance). We use the structured captions of these evaluation set videos as prompts and generate samples across 3 seeds per prompt at 480p (16:9) resolution. We produce a 5 s clip for each prompt.

We score each clip on Video Quality (VQ; DOVER perceptual quality score (Wu et al., 2023a)) and Dynamic Degree (DD; motion presence on a 0–1 scale (Huang et al., 2024)). From the three-seed DD scores per prompt (p), we compute a normalized motion control (MC) term

MC indicates the robustness of the control mechanism, \ie, the degree of variability per prompt for each control setting. We combine these into a Motion Fidelity score

where DDref is the per-band mean DD over the real-video reference set. The final Composite Score is the product of Video Quality and Motion Fidelity, reflecting adherence to motion magnitude without impacting the perceptual quality of generated videos. This is computed as \mathbb{E}_{\text{FPS-band}}\!\left[(\text{VQ})\cdot\text{MF}\right], computed per FPS band and then averaged across bands.

Tab. 29 reports averages across the four FPS bands. Both mechanisms improve over Base individually; MRoPE FPS modulation alone yields a larger gain than the Text Control (+1.12 vs. +0.77 in composite). Combining the two produces the best composite score (+1.30 over Base). VQ stays within a 0.2-point window across all four settings, indicating that the gains are concentrated in motion fidelity rather than video perceptual quality, \ie, the controls primarily improve temporal behavior. Based on these results, we adopt the Text Control + MRoPE FPS Modulation configuration for Cosmos 3 Generator.

Table 29: FPS control ablation on Cosmos3-Nano. Scores are averaged across four FPS bands (10, 15, 24, 30). VQ is the DOVER video quality score; MF is motion fidelity (0–1); Composite =\mathbb{E}_{\text{band}}[(\text{VQ})\cdot\text{MF}]. Bold indicates best in the column. Text Control + MRoPE FPS Modulation is the most performant control setting that demonstrates adherence to reference FPS band motion while preserving perceptual quality.

We investigate the impact of including audio during continued pre-training on video metrics. Starting from the same pre-trained checkpoint, we train two Cosmos3-Nano variants on our pre-training dataset: one with video-only data and one with joint video-audio data. These ablations are run for 20k iterations on 128 GPUs. We restrict training to 256p and 480p resolutions.

Table 30: Effect of introducing audio data during pre-training. We report PAIBench T2V and I2V scores after continued pre-training of two generator variants that differ only in whether audio is used during training. The video data is shared across both experiments.

The results in Tab. 30 show that continued training without audio leads to a drop in both T2V and I2V scores, suggesting that joint video-audio pre-training does not degrade video generation quality and may provide a modest benefit even when evaluated purely on video-centric metrics.

As described in Sec. 2.2.2 and summarized in Fig. 4, Cosmos 3 supports three action generation modes: forward dynamics (FD), inverse dynamics (ID), and joint video-action prediction (policy). We ablate whether a single joint action model can share useful structure across these modes. We use the PushT dataset and Cosmos3-Edge for this experiment. The model is trained for three single-mode action checkpoints for 2K steps each against one joint FD/ID/policy checkpoint trained for 6K steps, so that each mode is trained for the same amount of optimization steps. We report the PSNR for FD and MSE for ID. For policy mode, we report the policy coverage ratio of the T block and target region aggregated across 50 different initializations, with 10 rollouts from each starting point. The results are summarized in Tab. 31.

Table 31: PushT action-mode synergy. We compare single-mode FD, ID, and policy checkpoints trained for 2K steps each against one joint FD/ID/policy checkpoint trained for 6K steps. Lower is better for ID MSE; higher is better for FD PSNR and policy coverage. Bold indicates the better value in each column.

The joint FD/ID/policy checkpoint improves the action-side metrics while preserving comparable forward-dynamics quality. Compared with the single-mode checkpoints, ID MSE decreases from 1.11×10−3 to 3.09×10−4, a 72% relative reduction, and policy coverage increases from 74.1% to 77.3%. FD PSNR decreases from 27.13 to 26.22, indicating a modest tradeoff in reconstruction fidelity. Overall, the joint checkpoint provides the best policy coverage and ID accuracy under the same per-mode optimization budget, suggesting that the action modes share useful structure even though FD quality benefits slightly from single-mode specialization.

In addition to the closed-loop success rate reported in Sec. 6.2.5, we evaluate how well the video and action streams jointly predicted by Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID remain aligned on RoboLab. Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID is trained only on DROID, so RoboLab provides a held-out environment for testing this video-action consistency. For each predicted action chunk, we execute the same chunk in the RoboLab simulator and compute PSNR between the model-predicted video and the resulting simulator rollout, then aggregate the scores across action chunks for the left and wrist camera views. The left third-person view achieves 23.19 dB, comparable to the PSNR levels achieved by our robotics forward-dynamics models on DROID (Tab. 18). The wrist (eye-in-hand) view is more challenging because the camera moves with the end-effector and the model must infer newly revealed content; nevertheless, it reaches 17.33 dB. These results indicate strong consistency between the predicted actions and predicted videos. Figure 37 visualizes this consistency: the predicted frames closely match the corresponding frames from simulator rollouts initialized from the same state.

Figure 37: Predicted video vs. simulator rollout on RoboLab. For the wrist and left cameras, Sim Env shows the video recorded by executing the predicted action chunk in the RoboLab simulator from the same initial state, while Pred shows the video predicted by Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID jointly with that action chunk. We observe that the predicted video closely matches the simulator rollout.

Cosmos-HumanEval (Cosmos-HUE or HUE) is an evaluation benchmark for video generation introduced in the main results section. HUE provides a human-reference signal via atomic binary questions generated per video by a Vision-Language Model (VLM) pipeline and scored along the four HUE dimensions (Semantic Alignment, Physical Laws, Geometric Reasoning, Visual Integrity). This appendix complements that overview with the formal binary scoring scheme, the annotation protocol and reliability estimates, and the per-dimension and per-domain Text-to-Video (T2V) and Image-to-Video (I2V) leaderboards.

Each Layer 3 question elicits Yes (criterion met), No (clear violation), or Unclear (e.g., the region is occluded or the motion is too fast to assess, or the video fails to depict the event the question presupposes, e.g., the prompt calls for a right turn but the lead vehicle never turns, so the follow-up question about a smooth curved arc has no clear Yes or No). Unclear is treated as No: a model is not rewarded for failing to produce the prompted action, and a non-confident annotator is conservatively counted against the model. Concretely, Unclear does not contribute to the Yes numerator but remains in the denominator, so a video that is mostly Unclear cannot score above one with the same number of explicit Yes answers. Let \mathcal{Q}_{v} denote the set of questions issued for video v; the per-video HUE score is

with HUE⁡(v)∈[0,100]% since “Yes” is always the desirable outcome. Model-level scores aggregate over V test videos:

The grand mean weights every answered (video, question) observation equally, avoiding inflation from videos that happen to receive fewer applicable questions. Dimension-level scores are computed identically by restricting the sums to questions belonging to each dimension.

Each video receives up to 16 atomic binary questions from the three-layer pipeline above, and each (video, question) pair is independently rated by two human annotators. If the two annotators agree, the consensus answer is recorded as the canonical response; if they disagree, the question is escalated to a third quality-control (QC) reviewer, whose answer is final. This double-rating + QC-tiebreaker workflow yields a single canonical answer per (video, question) pair, bounds the contribution of any single annotator, and produces the auditable response stream that the scoring formulas in Equations 12–13 operate on.

Authoring and refining atomic questions targets two goals: low variance (re-running the same model on the same prompts produces a similar score), and GT saturation (real videos paired with the prompts score at or near 100%). We use these criteria to evaluate candidate questions and to iterate the question bank, revising or dropping items that fail any criterion. The process is ongoing: the GT score remains below 100% (Tabs. 32 and 33), so question-bank refinement continues.

The current T2V evaluation pool samples 100 prompts from PAIBench-G, with 5 random-seed generations per prompt and up to 20 questions per video, yielding up to 10,000 binary observations per model checkpoint. Treating each as an independent Bernoulli trial with underlying Yes-rate p=HUE⁡(m)/100, the 95% confidence interval on the model-level HUE score (in percentage points) is \mathrm{HUE}(m)\pm 100\cdot 1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/N} with N the observation count; in practice this gives CI95 widths around ±0.6 points for top-tier scores on the scale of Tab. 32. Atomic binary judgments reduce within-annotator variance compared to Likert-scale grading, where the annotator must integrate multiple observations, weigh them, and map onto an arbitrary scale. Each of these three operations introduces noise. The Real video GT row scores 93.6 on T2V prompts and 94.4 on I2V prompts, reflecting (i) minor residual prompt–video mismatches in the sampled PAIBench-G pairs despite manual review, and (ii) imperfections in the auto-generated question set, where overly strict, ambiguous, or off-target questions can yield No or Unclear on a real video. We treat the gap from GT to 100% as a north-star for ongoing question-bank refinement.

Tab. 32 reports current T2V results across our model panel and the strongest external T2V baselines. Veo-3.1 leads overall (91.3) and Seedance-1.5-Pro is second (90.0); Cosmos3-Super is the best open-source generator at 89.3, ahead of Wan2.2-A14B (88.2) and Cosmos3-Nano (87.6). The per-dimension picture is more favorable to Cosmos3-Super: it is the best open-source model on 9 of 12 axes, and beats every generator, including closed-source, on AV (87.7) and Physics (91.5). The gap from the strongest generator to real video (Real video GT, 93.6) is ∼2.3 points overall, leaving meaningful headroom for the next round.

Tab. 33 reports the parallel I2V evaluation. Veo-3.1 leads overall (89.7), with Cosmos3-Super trailing by only 0.1 points (89.6); Cosmos3-Nano (88.6) edges Wan2.2-A14B (88.4) and Seedance-1.5-Pro (87.6). Cosmos3-Super beats every generator outright on Visual Integrity (94.2), Robotics (91.1), and Miscellaneous (94.8), and ties Veo-3.1 for the lead on Semantic Alignment (both 90.3); Cosmos3-Nano wins AV (87.6) outright; Wan2.2-A14B wins Physics (91.9). The full I2V slate spans ∼9 points across generators.

Table 32: Cosmos HUE T2V leaderboard. Per-dimension and per-domain breakdowns (%; higher is better). Left block: Overall HUE plus the four dimensions (Semantic Alignment, Physical Laws, Geometric Reasoning, Visual Integrity). Right block (after the rule): Overall HUE restricted to each PAIBench-G prompt domain (C.S., AV, Rob., Ind., Hum., Phy., Misc. abbreviate Common Sense, Autonomous Vehicle, Robotics, Industry, Human, Physics, Miscellaneous). Cosmos 3 generators (ours) are shaded green; Real video GT is the upper reference. Bold marks the best in the column, underline the second best. #9809. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9808. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

#9806. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#9805. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9804. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9803. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9802. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#9800. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.
